happy-life_section-01.originalText: All men, brother Gallio, wish to live happily, but are dull at perceiving exactly what it is that makes life happy: and so far is it from being easy to attain to happiness that the more eagerly a man struggles to reach it the further he departs from it, if he takes the wrong road; for, since this leads in the opposite direction, his very swiftness carries him all the further away. We must therefore first define clearly what it is at which we aim: next we must consider by what path we may most speedily reach it, for on our journey itself, provided it be made in the right direction, we shall learn how much progress we have made each day, and how much nearer we are to the goal towards which our natural desires urge us.
happy-life_section-01.plainEnglish: All people, brother Gallio, want to live happily. But they're terrible at figuring out what actually makes life happy. It's so hard to reach happiness that the harder you chase it, the further away you get — if you're going the wrong way. When you're on the wrong road, your speed just carries you further from where you want to be. So first we need to define clearly what we're aiming for. Then we need to figure out the best path to get there. Once we're on the right path, we'll be able to see our daily progress and how much closer we're getting to the goal that our nature pushes us toward.

happy-life_section-01.originalText: But as long as we wander at random, not following any guide except the shouts and discordant clamours of those who invite us to proceed in different directions, our short life will be wasted in useless roamings, even if we labour both day and night to get a good understanding. Let us not therefore decide whither we must tend, and by what path, without the advice of some experienced person who has explored the region which we are about to enter, because this journey is not subject to the same conditions as others; for in them some distinctly understood track and inquiries made of the natives make it impossible for us to go wrong, but here the most beaten and frequented tracks are those which lead us most astray.
happy-life_section-01.plainEnglish: As long as we wander around without direction, following nothing but the shouting and conflicting noise of people pulling us in different directions, we'll waste our short lives in pointless wandering. This happens even when we work day and night to understand things better. So we shouldn't decide where to go or what path to take without advice from someone experienced — someone who has already explored the territory we're about to enter. This journey isn't like other trips. On regular trips, you can follow clear roads and ask locals for directions to avoid getting lost. But in life, the most popular and crowded paths are exactly the ones that lead us furthest astray.

happy-life_section-01.originalText: Nothing, therefore, is more important than that we should not, like sheep, follow the flock that has gone before us, and thus proceed not whither we ought, but whither the rest are going. Now nothing gets us into greater troubles than our subservience to common rumour, and our habit of thinking that those things are best which are most generally received as such, of taking many counterfeits for truly good things, and of living not by reason but by imitation of others. This is the cause of those great heaps into which men rush till they are piled one upon another. In a great crush of people, when the crowd presses upon itself, no one can fall without drawing some one else down upon him, and those who go before cause the destruction of those who follow them.
happy-life_section-01.plainEnglish: Nothing is more important than this: don't follow the crowd like sheep. Don't go where everyone else is going instead of where you should go. Nothing causes more trouble than listening to popular opinion. We think something must be good just because most people say it is. We mistake fake things for real ones. We live by copying others instead of using our own minds. This is why people pile up in great heaps, rushing forward until they're crushed together. In a mob, when the crowd presses in on itself, no one can fall without pulling someone else down. The people in front destroy the ones following behind.

happy-life_section-01.originalText: You may observe the same thing in human life: no one can merely go wrong by himself, but he must become both the cause and adviser of another's wrongdoing. It is harmful to follow the march of those who go before us, and since every one had rather believe another than form his own opinion, we never pass a deliberate judgment upon life, but some traditional error always entangles us and brings us to ruin, and we perish because we follow other men's examples: we should be cured of this if we were to disengage ourselves from the herd; but as it is, the mob is ready to fight against reason in defence of its own mistake. Consequently the same thing happens as at elections, where, when the fickle breeze of popular favour has veered round, those who have been chosen consuls and praetors are viewed with admiration by the very men who made them so. That we should all approve and disapprove of the same things is the end of every decision which is given according to the voice of the majority.
happy-life_section-01.plainEnglish: You can see the same pattern in human life: no one just makes mistakes alone. They end up causing others to go wrong and encouraging them to do it too. It's dangerous to follow the crowd that marches ahead of us. Since everyone would rather believe someone else than think for themselves, we never make careful judgments about how to live. Instead, some inherited mistake always traps us and destroys us. We die because we copy other people's examples. We could cure this problem if we broke away from the herd. But instead, the crowd is ready to fight reason itself to defend its own errors. The same thing happens in elections. When the fickle wind of popular opinion shifts, the very people who elected the consuls and praetors suddenly admire them. That we all approve and disapprove of the same things — this is what happens with every decision made by majority vote.

happy-life_section-02.originalText: When we are considering a happy life, you cannot answer me as though after a division of the House, "This view has most supporters;" because for that very reason it is the worse of the two: matters do not stand so well with mankind that the majority should prefer the better course: the more people do a thing the worse it is likely to be. Let us therefore inquire, not what is most commonly done, but what is best for us to do, and what will establish us in the possession of undying happiness, not what is approved of by the vulgar, the worst possible exponents of truth. By "the vulgar" I mean both those who wear woollen cloaks and those who wear crowns; for I do not regard the colour of the clothes with which they are covered: I do not trust my eyes to tell me what a man is: I have a better and more trustworthy light by which I can distinguish what is true from what is false: let the mind find out what is good for the mind.
happy-life_section-02.plainEnglish: When we're talking about the happy life, you can't just tell me "Most people agree with this view" as if we were voting in Congress. That's exactly why it's probably wrong. Things aren't going so well with humanity that the majority picks the better path. In fact, the more people do something, the worse it usually is. So let's ask a different question. Not "What do most people do?" but "What should we do? What will give us lasting happiness?" Don't ask what the masses approve of — they're terrible guides to truth. And by "the masses" I mean both the poor in wool cloaks and the rich wearing crowns. I don't judge people by their clothes. I don't trust my eyes to tell me who someone really is. I have a better, more reliable light to tell truth from lies: let the mind discover what's good for the mind.

happy-life_section-02.originalText: If a man ever allows his mind some breathing space and has leisure for communing with himself, what truths he will confess to himself, after having been put to the torture by his own self! He will say, "Whatever I have hitherto done I wish were undone: when I think over what I have said, I envy dumb people: whatever I have longed for seems to have been what my enemies would pray might befall me: good heaven, how far more endurable what I have feared seems to be than what I have lusted after. I have been at enmity with many men, and have changed my dislike of them into friendship, if friendship can exist between bad men: yet I have not yet become reconciled to myself.
happy-life_section-02.plainEnglish: If a man ever gives his mind some room to breathe and has time to be alone with himself, what truths he will admit to himself! It's like being tortured by his own thoughts. He will say, "I wish I could undo everything I've done so far. When I think about what I've said, I envy people who can't speak. Everything I've wanted seems like something my enemies would pray would happen to me. Good God, what I feared turns out to be so much more bearable than what I craved. I've been enemies with many people, then turned my hatred into friendship — if you can call it friendship when both people are bad. But I still haven't made peace with myself.

happy-life_section-02.originalText: I have striven with all my strength to raise myself above the common herd, and to make myself remarkable for some talent: what have I effected save to make myself a mark for the arrows of my enemies, and show those who hate me where to wound me? Do you see those who praise your eloquence, who covet your wealth, who court your favour, or who vaunt your power? All these either are, or, which comes to the same thing, may be your enemies: the number of those who envy you is as great as that of those who admire you; why do I not rather seek for some good thing which I can use and feel, not one which I can show? these good things which men gaze at in wonder, which they crowd to see, which one points out to another with speechless admiration, are outwardly brilliant, but within are miseries to those who possess them."
happy-life_section-02.plainEnglish: I worked as hard as I could to rise above ordinary people. I wanted to stand out for some special talent. But what did I accomplish? I just made myself a target for my enemies. I showed them exactly where to hurt me. Look around you. See those people who praise your speaking skills? The ones who want your money, seek your favor, or brag about your power? They're all your enemies. Or they might as well be. For every person who admires you, there's someone who envies you. So why don't I look for something good that I can actually use and enjoy? Something that's mine, not something to show off? These flashy things that people stare at in wonder — the things crowds gather to see, that leave people speechless with admiration — they shine on the outside. But inside, they make their owners miserable.

happy-life_section-03.originalText: Let us seek for some blessing, which does not merely look fine, but is sound and good throughout alike, and most beautiful in the parts which are least seen: let us unearth this. It is not far distant from us; it can be discovered: all that is necessary is to know whither to stretch out your hand: but, as it is, we behave as though we were in the dark, and reach out beyond what is nearest to us, striking as we do so against the very things that we want.
happy-life_section-03.plainEnglish: Let's look for something truly good — not just something that looks impressive, but something that is solid and genuine all the way through. Something most beautiful in the hidden parts that no one else sees. Let's dig this up. It's not far from us. It can be found. You just need to know where to reach for it. But instead, we act like we're stumbling around in the dark. We reach past what's right in front of us, and we end up knocking over the very things we actually want.

happy-life_section-03.originalText: However, that I may not draw you into digressions, I will pass over the opinions of other philosophers, because it would take a long time to state and confute them all: take ours. When, however, I say "ours," I do not bind myself to any one of the chiefs of the Stoic school, for I too have a right to form my own opinion. I shall, therefore, follow the authority of some of them, but shall ask some others to discriminate their meaning: perhaps, when after having reported all their opinions, I am asked for my own, I shall impugn none of my predecessors' decisions, and shall say, "I will also add somewhat to them."
happy-life_section-03.plainEnglish: But I don't want to drag you through endless side topics. I'll skip over what other philosophers think, since it would take forever to list and argue against all their views. Let's focus on our school instead. When I say 'our school,' I don't mean I'm locked into following any single Stoic leader. I have the right to think for myself too. I'll follow some of their ideas, but I'll ask others to clarify what they really mean. Maybe after I've shared all their views and you ask for mine, I won't attack any of my predecessors. Instead, I'll say, 'Let me add something to what they've said.'

happy-life_section-03.originalText: Meanwhile I follow nature, which is a point upon which every one of the Stoic philosophers are agreed: true wisdom consists in not departing from nature and in moulding our conduct according to her laws and model. A happy life, therefore, is one which is in accordance with its own nature, and cannot be brought about unless in the first place the mind be sound and remain so without interruption, and next, be bold and vigorous, enduring all things with most admirable courage, suited to the times in which it lives, careful of the body and its appurtenances, yet not troublesomely careful. It must also set due value upon all the things which adorn our lives, without over-estimating any one of them, and must be able to enjoy the bounty of Fortune without becoming her slave.
happy-life_section-03.plainEnglish: I follow nature, which all Stoic philosophers agree is the right path. True wisdom means staying close to nature and living by her rules. A happy life is one that fits with your own nature. But this can only happen if your mind is healthy and stays that way. Your mind must also be bold and strong, facing everything with courage. You need to adapt to your times. Care for your body and what it needs, but don't obsess over it. Value the good things in life without thinking any one thing is everything. And enjoy what fortune gives you without becoming its slave.

happy-life_section-03.originalText: You understand without my mentioning it that an unbroken calm and freedom ensue, when we have driven away all those things which either excite us or alarm us: for in the place of sensual pleasures and those slight perishable matters which are connected with the basest crimes, we thus gain an immense, unchangeable, equable joy, together with peace, calmness and greatness of mind, and kindliness: for all savageness is a sign of weakness.
happy-life_section-03.plainEnglish: You already know what happens when we push away everything that excites us or scares us. We find an unbroken calm and freedom. Instead of chasing physical pleasures and those cheap, temporary things that come with terrible crimes, we gain something huge: a joy that never changes or wavers. We also get peace, calmness, and greatness of mind. Plus kindliness — because all cruelty comes from weakness.

happy-life_section-04.originalText: Our highest good may also be defined otherwise, that is to say, the same idea may be expressed in different language. Just as the same army may at one time be extended more widely, at another contracted into a smaller compass, and may either be curved towards the wings by a depression in the line of the centre, or drawn up in a straight line, while, in whatever figure it be arrayed, its strength and loyalty remain unchanged; so also our definition of the highest good may in some cases be expressed diffusely and at great length, while in others it is put into a short and concise form. Thus, it will come to the same thing, if I say "The highest good is a mind which despises the accidents of fortune, and takes pleasure in virtue": or, "It is an unconquerable strength of mind, knowing the world well, gentle in its dealings, showing great courtesy and consideration for those with whom it is brought into contact."
happy-life_section-04.plainEnglish: We can define our highest good in different ways. The same idea can be expressed with different words. Think of an army — it might spread out wide or pull together tight. It might curve its wings back or form a straight line. No matter how it's arranged, its strength and loyalty stay the same. Our definition of the highest good works the same way. Sometimes we can explain it with many words. Other times we can say it briefly. Both ways mean the same thing. I could say, 'The highest good is a mind that ignores the ups and downs of fortune and finds joy in virtue.' Or I could say, 'It's an unbeatable strength of mind that understands the world well, acts gently, and treats everyone with courtesy and kindness.'

happy-life_section-04.originalText: Or we may choose to define it by calling that man happy who knows good and bad only in the form of good or bad minds: who worships honour, and is satisfied with his own virtue, who is neither puffed up by good fortune nor cast down by evil fortune, who knows no other good than that which he is able to bestow upon himself, whose real pleasure lies in despising pleasures. If you choose to pursue this digression further, you can put this same idea into many other forms, without impairing or weakening its meaning: for what prevents our saying that a happy life consists in a mind which is free, upright, undaunted, and steadfast, beyond the influence of fear or desire, which thinks nothing good except honour, and nothing bad except shame, and regards everything else as a mass of mean details which can neither add anything to nor take anything away from the happiness of life, but which come and go without either increasing or diminishing the highest good?
happy-life_section-04.plainEnglish:
Or we could define it this way: the happy person only sees good and bad in terms of character. They value honor above all else and find satisfaction in their own virtue. Good luck doesn't make them proud. Bad luck doesn't crush them. They know that the only real good is what they can give themselves. Their true pleasure comes from not needing pleasures.

You could express this same idea many different ways without changing its meaning. What's stopping us from saying that a happy life means having a mind that is free, honest, fearless, and steady? A mind that fear and desire can't touch? One that considers nothing good except honor, and nothing bad except shame? Everything else is just trivial details that can't add to or subtract from your happiness. These things come and go, but they never increase or decrease what truly matters.

happy-life_section-04.originalText: A man of these principles, whether he will or no, must be accompanied by a continual cheerfulness, a high happiness, which comes indeed from on high because he delights in what he has, and desires no greater pleasures than those which his home affords. Is he not right in allowing these to turn the scale against petty, ridiculous, and shortlived movements of his wretched body? on the day on which he becomes proof against pleasure he also becomes proof against pain. See, on the other hand, how evil and guilty a slavery the man is forced to serve who is dominated in turn by pleasures and pains, those most untrustworthy and passionate of masters.
happy-life_section-04.plainEnglish: A person who lives by these principles will naturally be cheerful and deeply happy. This happiness comes from above because he enjoys what he has. He doesn't want pleasures greater than what his own life provides. Isn't he right to let this happiness outweigh the small, silly, temporary troubles of his weak body? The day he becomes immune to pleasure, he also becomes immune to pain. Look at the opposite: how terrible and shameful it is to be enslaved by pleasures and pains — those unreliable and violent masters.

happy-life_section-04.originalText: We must, therefore, escape from them into freedom. This nothing will bestow upon us save contempt of Fortune: but if we attain to this, then there will dawn upon us those invaluable blessings, the repose of a mind that is at rest in a safe haven, its lofty imaginings, its great and steady delight at casting out errors and learning to know the truth, its courtesy, and its cheerfulness, in all of which we shall take delight, not regarding them as good things, but as proceeding from the proper good of man.
happy-life_section-04.plainEnglish: We must escape from these troubles into freedom. Only one thing can give us this freedom: caring nothing about what Fortune does to us. If we achieve this, then priceless blessings will come to us. Our mind will find peace in a safe harbor. We'll have noble thoughts and great, steady joy as we cast out our mistakes and learn the truth. We'll be kind and cheerful. We'll delight in all of these — not because they are good in themselves, but because they flow from what is truly good in human nature.

happy-life_section-05.originalText: Since I have begun to make my definitions without a too strict adherence to the letter, a man may be called "happy" who, thanks to reason, has ceased either to hope or to fear: but rocks also feel neither fear nor sadness, nor do cattle, yet no one would call those things happy which cannot comprehend what happiness is. With them you may class men whose dull nature and want of self-knowledge reduces them to the level of cattle, mere animals: there is no difference between the one and the other, because the latter have no reason, while the former have only a corrupted form of it, crooked and cunning to their own hurt.
happy-life_section-05.plainEnglish: Since I've started defining things more loosely, we might call a man "happy" if reason has freed him from both hope and fear. But rocks don't feel fear or sadness either, and neither do cattle. Yet no one would call them happy, because they can't understand what happiness means. You can put in this same category those people whose dull minds and lack of self-knowledge reduce them to the level of cattle — basically animals. There's no real difference between them and actual beasts. Animals have no reason at all, while these people have reason that's been twisted and corrupted in ways that hurt them.

happy-life_section-05.originalText: For no one can be styled happy who is beyond the influence of truth: and consequently a happy life is unchangeable, and is founded upon a true and trustworthy discernment; for the mind is uncontaminated and freed from all evils only when it is able to escape not merely from wounds but also from scratches, when it will always be able to maintain the position which it has taken up, and defend it even against the angry assaults of Fortune:
happy-life_section-05.plainEnglish: No one can be truly happy if they live in delusion. Real happiness never wavers — it's built on clear, reliable judgment. Your mind is only pure and free from all troubles when it can avoid not just major wounds but even small scratches. When you reach this point, you can hold your ground no matter what and defend it even when Fortune attacks you with fury.

happy-life_section-05.originalText: for with regard to sensual pleasures, though they were to surround one on every side, and use every means of assault, trying to win over the mind by caresses and making trial of every conceivable stratagem to attract either our entire selves or our separate parts, yet what mortal that retains any traces of human origin would wish to be tickled day and night, and, neglecting his mind, to devote himself to bodily enjoyments?
happy-life_section-05.plainEnglish: Think about physical pleasures for a moment. Imagine they surrounded you completely and tried every trick to win you over. They flatter you and tempt every part of your body and soul. Even then, what person with any human dignity would want to be entertained day and night? Who would ignore their mind just to focus on bodily pleasures?

happy-life_section-06.originalText:
“But,” says our adversary, “the mind also will have pleasures
of its own.” Let it have them, then, and let it sit in judgment
over luxury and pleasures; let it indulge itself to the full in all
those matters which give sensual delights: then let it look back
upon what it enjoyed before, and with all those faded sensualities
fresh in its memory let it rejoice and look eagerly forward to those
other pleasures which it experienced long ago, and intends to
experience again, and while the body lies in helpless repletion in
the present, let it send its thoughts onward towards the future,
and take stock of its hopes: all this will make it appear, in my
opinion, yet more wretched, because it is insanity to choose evil
instead of good: now no insane person can be happy, and no one can
be sane if he regards what is injurious as the highest good and
strives to obtain it.
happy-life_section-06.plainEnglish: "But," our opponent says, "the mind will have its own pleasures too." Fine, let it have them. Let the mind judge luxury and pleasure. Let it indulge completely in everything that feels good to the senses. Then let it look back at what it enjoyed before. Let it remember all those faded sensations and feel happy about them. Let it eagerly look forward to pleasures it experienced long ago and plans to experience again. While the body lies there stuffed and helpless in the present, let the mind send its thoughts toward the future and count up its hopes. All of this will make it seem even more miserable, in my opinion. Why? Because it's madness to choose evil over good. No insane person can be happy. And no one can be sane if they think harmful things are the highest good and work to get them.

happy-life_section-06.originalText:
The happy man, therefore, is he who can make
a right judgment in all things: he is happy who in his present
circumstances, whatever they may be, is satisfied and on friendly
terms with the conditions of his life. That man is happy, whose
reason recommends to him the whole posture of his affairs.
happy-life_section-06.plainEnglish: So who is the happy man? He's someone who can judge things correctly. He's happy when he accepts his current situation, whatever it is, and makes peace with his life as it stands. The happy man is the one whose reason tells him that everything in his life is as it should be.

happy-life_section-07.originalText: Even those very people who declare the highest good to be in the belly, see what a dishonourable position they have assigned to it: and therefore they say that pleasure cannot be parted from virtue, and that no one can either live honourably without living cheerfully, nor yet live cheerfully without living honourably. I do not see how these very different matters can have any connexion with one another. What is there, I pray you, to prevent virtue existing apart from pleasure? of course the reason is that all good things derive their origin from virtue, and therefore even those things which you cherish and seek for come originally from its roots.
happy-life_section-07.plainEnglish: Even people who say the highest good is physical pleasure realize how shameful that sounds. So they claim that pleasure can't be separated from virtue. They say no one can live with honor without being happy, and no one can be happy without living with honor. I don't see how these totally different things connect at all. What stops virtue from existing without pleasure? The truth is that all good things come from virtue. Even the things you love and chase after originally grow from virtue's roots.

happy-life_section-07.originalText: Yet, if they were entirely inseparable, we should not see some things to be pleasant, but not honourable, and others most honourable indeed, but hard and only to be attained by suffering. Add to this, that pleasure visits the basest lives, but virtue cannot co-exist with an evil life; yet some unhappy people are not without pleasure, nay, it is owing to pleasure itself that they are unhappy; and this could not take place if pleasure had any connexion with virtue, whereas virtue is often without pleasure, and never stands in need of it.
happy-life_section-07.plainEnglish: But if pleasure and virtue were truly inseparable, we wouldn't see some things that feel good but are wrong, and other things that are clearly right but difficult and painful to achieve. Consider this: pleasure visits the worst kinds of lives, but virtue cannot exist alongside an evil life. Some miserable people still experience pleasure — in fact, it's often pleasure itself that makes them miserable. This couldn't happen if pleasure had any real connection to virtue. Virtue often exists without pleasure and never needs it.

happy-life_section-07.originalText: Why do you put together two things which are unlike and even incompatible one with another? virtue is a lofty quality, sublime, royal, unconquerable, untiring: pleasure is low, slavish, weakly, perishable; its haunts and homes are the brothel and the tavern. You will meet virtue in the temple, the market-place, the senate house, manning the walls, covered with dust, sunburnt, horny-handed: you will find pleasure skulking out of sight, seeking for shady nooks at the public baths, hot chambers, and places which dread the visits of the aedile, soft, effeminate, reeking of wine and perfumes, pale or perhaps painted and made up with cosmetics.
happy-life_section-07.plainEnglish: Why are you trying to combine two things that are completely different and don't belong together? Virtue is noble, majestic, kingly, unbeatable, and tireless. Pleasure is low, servile, weak, and temporary. Pleasure lives in brothels and bars. You'll find virtue in temples, the marketplace, the senate — standing guard on the walls, dusty, sunburned, with calloused hands. You'll find pleasure hiding in the shadows, lurking in shady corners of bathhouses, in heated rooms, and places that fear visits from the police. Pleasure is soft, feminine, reeking of wine and perfume, pale or caked with makeup.

happy-life_section-07.originalText: The highest good is immortal: it knows no ending, and does not admit of either satiety or regret: for a right-thinking mind never alters or becomes hateful to itself, nor do the best things ever undergo any change: but pleasure dies at the very moment when it charms us most: it has no great scope, and therefore it soon cloys and wearies us, and fades away as soon as its first impulse is over: indeed, we cannot depend upon anything whose nature is to change. Consequently it is not even possible that there should be any solid substance in that which comes and goes so swiftly, and which perishes by the very exercise of its own functions, for it arrives at a point at which it ceases to be, and even while it is beginning always keeps its end in view.
happy-life_section-07.plainEnglish: The highest good lasts forever. It never ends, and it never makes us sick of it or sorry we chose it. A right-thinking mind never changes or starts to hate itself. The best things never change. But pleasure dies the moment it delights us most. It doesn't have much room to grow, so it quickly becomes boring and tiresome. It fades away as soon as its first rush is over. We can't count on anything that keeps changing by nature. So there can't be any real substance in something that comes and goes so fast. It destroys itself by its very activity. It reaches a point where it stops existing. Even while it's starting, it's already looking toward its own end.

happy-life_section-08.originalText: What answer are we to make to the reflexion that pleasure belongs to good and bad men alike, and that bad men take as much delight in their shame as good men in noble things? This was why the ancients bade us lead the highest, not the most pleasant life, in order that pleasure might not be the guide but the companion of a right-thinking and honourable mind; for it is Nature whom we ought to make our guide: let our reason watch her, and be advised by her. To live happily, then, is the same thing as to live according to Nature: what this may be, I will explain.
happy-life_section-08.plainEnglish: But here's a problem: both good and bad people experience pleasure. Bad people enjoy their shameful acts just as much as good people enjoy doing noble things. This is why ancient philosophers told us to aim for the highest life, not the most pleasant one. Pleasure shouldn't be our guide — it should just come along for the ride when we think and act honorably. Nature should be our guide instead. Let reason keep watch over nature and take its advice. So living happily is the same as living according to nature. Let me explain what this means.

happy-life_section-08.originalText: If we guard the endowments of the body and the advantages of nature with care and fearlessness, as things soon to depart and given to us only for a day; if we do not fall under their dominion, nor allow ourselves to become the slaves of what is no part of our own being; if we assign to all bodily pleasures and external delights the same position which is held by auxiliaries and light-armed troops in a camp; if we make them our servants, not our masters—then and then only are they of value to our minds.
happy-life_section-08.plainEnglish: We should protect our physical health and natural gifts with care, but without fear. Remember they won't last long — they're only on loan to us for a short time. Don't let them control you. Don't become a slave to things that aren't really part of who you are. Think of bodily pleasures and external comforts like support troops in an army — useful helpers, but not the main force. Make them serve you, not the other way around. Only then do they actually help your mind.

happy-life_section-08.originalText: A man should be unbiassed and not to be conquered by external things: he ought to admire himself alone, to feel confidence in his own spirit, and so to order his life as to be ready alike for good or for bad fortune. Let not his confidence be without knowledge, nor his knowledge without steadfastness: let him always abide by what he has once determined, and let there be no erasure in his doctrines. It will be understood, even though I append it not, that such a man will be tranquil and composed in his demeanour, high-minded and courteous in his actions.
happy-life_section-08.plainEnglish: A person should stay neutral and not let outside forces control them. They should respect themselves alone and trust their own judgment. They should live ready for whatever comes — good times or bad. But don't let confidence become ignorance, and don't let knowledge become weakness. Always stick to what you've decided. Don't keep changing your principles. It goes without saying that this kind of person will be calm and steady. They'll act with dignity and treat others well.

happy-life_section-08.originalText: Let reason be encouraged by the senses to seek for the truth, and draw its first principles from thence: indeed it has no other base of operations or place from which to start in pursuit of truth: it must fall back upon itself. Even the all-embracing universe and God who is its guide extends himself forth into outward things, and yet altogether returns from all sides back to himself. Let our mind do the same thing: when, following its bodily senses it has by means of them sent itself forth into the things of the outward world, let it remain still their master and its own.
happy-life_section-08.plainEnglish: Let reason learn from your senses as it searches for truth. Your senses give reason its starting point — it has nowhere else to begin. Without them, reason can only circle back on itself. Even the vast universe and the God who guides it reaches out into all things, yet always returns to itself from every direction. Our minds should work the same way. When your mind follows your bodily senses out into the external world, let it stay in control — both of them and of itself.

happy-life_section-08.originalText: By this means we shall obtain a strength and an ability which are united and allied together, and shall derive from it that reason which never halts between two opinions, nor is dull in forming its perceptions, beliefs, or convictions. Such a mind, when it has ranged itself in order, made its various parts agree together, and, if I may so express myself, harmonized them, has attained to the highest good: for it has nothing evil or hazardous remaining, nothing to shake it or make it stumble: it will do everything under the guidance of its own will, and nothing unexpected will befal it, but whatever may be done by it will turn out well, and that, too, readily and easily, without the doer having recourse to any underhand devices: for slow and hesitating action are the signs of discord and want of settled purpose. You may, then, boldly declare that the highest good is singleness of mind: for where agreement and unity are, there must the virtues be: it is the vices that are at war one with another.
happy-life_section-08.plainEnglish: This gives us strength and ability working together as allies. We get a mind that never wavers between two choices or gets confused about what to think or believe. When this mind organizes itself and makes all its parts work together in harmony, it reaches the highest good. It has nothing evil or dangerous left in it. Nothing can shake it or make it stumble. It will do everything by its own choice, and nothing will catch it off guard. Whatever it does will turn out well — quickly and easily, without any sneaky tricks. Slow, hesitant action shows inner conflict and confusion. So you can boldly say that the highest good is having a unified mind. Where there's agreement and unity, the virtues must be. It's the vices that fight against each other.

happy-life_section-09.originalText: "But," says our adversary, "you yourself only practise virtue because you hope to obtain some pleasure from it." In the first place, even though virtue may afford us pleasure, still we do not seek after her on that account: for she does not bestow this, but bestows this to boot, nor is this the end for which she labours, but her labour wins this also, although it be directed to another end. As in a tilled-field, when ploughed for corn, some flowers are found amongst it, and yet, though these posies may charm the eye, all this labour was not spent in order to produce them—the man who sowed the field had another object in view, he gained this over and above it—so pleasure is not the reward or the cause of virtue, but comes in addition to it; nor do we choose virtue because she gives us pleasure, but she gives us pleasure also if we choose her.
happy-life_section-09.plainEnglish: "But," our opponent says, "you yourself only practice virtue because you hope to get some pleasure from it." First, even if virtue does give us pleasure, that's still not why we pursue her. She doesn't offer pleasure as her main gift — she throws it in as a bonus. This isn't her goal, but her work happens to win this too, even though she's aimed at something else. It's like a plowed field planted for grain. You might find some flowers growing among the crops. These flowers may be beautiful, but all that hard work wasn't done to grow them. The farmer had a different goal in mind — he got the flowers as an extra. So pleasure isn't the reward or the reason for virtue. It just comes along with it. We don't choose virtue because she gives us pleasure. But if we do choose her, she gives us pleasure too.

happy-life_section-09.originalText: The highest good lies in the act of choosing her, and in the attitude of the noblest minds, which when once it has fulfilled its function and established itself within its own limits has attained to the highest good, and needs nothing more: for there is nothing outside of the whole, any more than there is anything beyond the end. You are mistaken, therefore, when you ask me what it is on account of which I seek after virtue: for you are seeking for something above the highest. Do you ask what I seek from virtue? I answer. Herself: for she has nothing better; she is her own reward.
happy-life_section-09.plainEnglish: The highest good lies in choosing virtue itself, and in the mindset of the noblest people. Once this mindset has done its job and settled within its proper bounds, it has reached the highest good and needs nothing more. There is nothing outside of the whole, just as there is nothing beyond the end. You are mistaken when you ask me why I pursue virtue. You're looking for something above the highest point. Do you ask what I seek from virtue? I answer: virtue herself. She has nothing better than herself. She is her own reward.

happy-life_section-09.originalText: Does this not appear great enough, when I tell you that the highest good is an unyielding strength of mind, wisdom, magnanimity, sound judgment, freedom, harmony, beauty? Do you still ask me for something greater, of which these may be regarded as the attributes? Why do you talk of pleasures to me? I am seeking to find what is good for man, not for his belly; why, cattle and whales have larger ones than he.
happy-life_section-09.plainEnglish: Isn't this impressive enough? I'm telling you that the highest good is unshakeable mental strength, wisdom, courage, sound judgment, freedom, harmony, and beauty. Do you still want something more? These are already the greatest qualities possible. Why do you keep talking to me about pleasures? I'm trying to find what's good for human beings, not for their stomachs. Animals have bigger bellies than we do.

happy-life_section-10.originalText: "You purposely misunderstand what I say," says he, "for I too say that no one can live pleasantly unless he lives honorably also, and this cannot be the case with dumb animals who measure the extent of their happiness by that of their food. I loudly and publicly proclaim that what I call a pleasant life cannot exist without the addition of virtue."
happy-life_section-10.plainEnglish: "You're deliberately twisting my words," he says. "I also say that no one can live pleasantly unless they live honorably too. Animals can't do this — they measure their happiness only by how much food they get. I loudly and publicly declare that what I call a pleasant life cannot exist without virtue."

happy-life_section-10.originalText: Yet who does not know that the greatest fools drink the deepest of those pleasures of yours? or that vice is full of enjoyments, and that the mind itself suggests to itself many perverted, vicious forms of pleasure?—in the first place arrogance, excessive self-esteem, swaggering precedence over other men, a shortsighted, nay, a blind devotion to his own interests, dissolute luxury, excessive delight springing from the most trifling and childish causes, and also talkativeness, pride that takes a pleasure in insulting others, sloth, and the decay of a dull mind which goes to sleep over itself.
happy-life_section-10.plainEnglish: But everyone knows that the biggest fools indulge most deeply in these pleasures you're talking about. Vice is packed with enjoyments. The mind comes up with all kinds of twisted, corrupt pleasures on its own. Like arrogance and thinking too highly of yourself. Like pushing ahead of others and caring only about yourself in the most narrow-minded, blind way. Like wasteful luxury and getting excited over the most trivial, childish things. And also endless talking, the kind of pride that enjoys insulting people, laziness, and letting your mind rot by doing nothing with it.

happy-life_section-10.originalText: All these are dissipated by virtue, which plucks a man by the ear, and measures the value of pleasures before she permits them to be used; nor does she set much store by those which she allows to pass current, for she merely allows their use, and her cheerfulness is not due to her use of them, but to her moderation in using them.
happy-life_section-10.plainEnglish: Virtue sweeps all these problems away. It grabs you by the ear and makes you think about whether pleasures are actually worth it before you indulge. And even the pleasures virtue approves? It doesn't think much of them. It just allows them. Virtue's happiness doesn't come from using these pleasures — it comes from using them wisely.

happy-life_section-10.originalText: "Yet when moderation lessens pleasure, it impairs the highest good." You devote yourself to pleasures, I check them; you indulge in pleasure, I use it; you think that it is the highest good, I do not even think it to be good: for the sake of pleasure I do nothing, you do everything.
happy-life_section-10.plainEnglish: "But when moderation reduces pleasure, it damages the highest good." You chase after pleasures, I hold them back. You dive into pleasure, I just sample it. You think pleasure is the ultimate goal, I don't even think it's good. I won't do anything just for pleasure, but you'll do anything for it.

happy-life_section-11.originalText: When I say that I do nothing for the sake of pleasure, I allude to that wise man, whom alone you admit to be capable of pleasure: now I do not call a man wise who is overcome by anything, let alone by pleasure: yet, if engrossed by pleasure, how will he resist toil, danger, want, and all the ills which surround and threaten the life of man? How will he bear the sight of death or of pain? How will he endure the tumult of the world, and make head against so many most active foes, if he be conquered by so effeminate an antagonist? He will do whatever pleasure advises him: well, do you not see how many things it will advise him to do?
happy-life_section-11.plainEnglish: When I say that I do nothing for the sake of pleasure, I'm talking about the wise man — the only person you admit can truly enjoy pleasure. But I don't call anyone wise if they can be conquered by anything, especially by pleasure. If pleasure has power over him, how will he resist hard work, danger, poverty, and all the troubles that surround human life? How will he face death or pain? How will he handle the chaos of the world and fight against so many fierce enemies, if he's been defeated by such a weak opponent? He'll do whatever pleasure tells him to do. Can't you see how many terrible things it will make him do?

happy-life_section-11.originalText: "It will not," says our adversary, "be able to give him any bad advice, because it is combined with virtue?" Again, do you not see what a poor kind of highest good that must be which requires a guardian to ensure its being good at all? and how is virtue to rule pleasure if she follows it, seeing that to follow is the duty of a subordinate, to rule that of a commander? do you put that which commands in the background? According to your school, virtue has the dignified office of preliminary taster of pleasures. We shall, however, see whether virtue still remains virtue among those who treat her with such contempt, for if she leaves her proper station she can no longer keep her proper name:
happy-life_section-11.plainEnglish: "It won't," says our opponent, "be able to give him bad advice, because it's combined with virtue." But don't you see what a weak kind of highest good this must be if it needs a guardian to make sure it stays good? And how can virtue rule pleasure if virtue follows pleasure around? The follower takes orders — the commander gives them. Are you really putting the one who should command in second place? According to your school of thought, virtue gets the dignified job of taste-testing pleasures first. But we'll see if virtue is still virtue when people treat her with such disrespect. If she abandons her proper position, she can no longer keep her proper name.

happy-life_section-11.originalText: in the meanwhile, to keep to the point, I will show you many men beset by pleasures, men upon whom Fortune has showered all her gifts, whom you must needs admit to be bad men. Look at Nomentanus and Apicius, who digest all the good things, as they call them, of the sea and land, and review upon their tables the whole animal kingdom. Look at them as they lie on beds of roses gloating over their banquet, delighting their ears with music, their eyes with exhibitions, their palates with flavours: their whole bodies are titillated with soft and soothing applications, and lest even their nostrils should be idle, the very place in which, they solemnize the rites of luxury is scented with various perfumes. You will say that these men live in the midst of pleasures. Yet they are ill at ease, because they take pleasure in what is not good.
happy-life_section-11.plainEnglish: But let me stick to the point. I can show you many men who are drowning in pleasures — men Fortune has blessed with everything. You'd have to admit these are bad men. Look at Nomentanus and Apicius. They devour all the "good things" from sea and land. They parade the entire animal kingdom across their dinner tables. Picture them lying on beds of roses, gloating over their feasts. They delight their ears with music, their eyes with shows, their tongues with exotic flavors. Their whole bodies are pampered with soft, soothing touches. And so their noses won't feel left out, they perfume the very rooms where they worship luxury. You'd say these men live surrounded by pleasures. Yet they're miserable — because they're taking pleasure in things that aren't actually good.

happy-life_section-12.originalText: "They are ill at ease," replies he, "because many things arise which distract their thoughts, and their minds are disquieted by conflicting opinions." I admit that this is true: still these very men, foolish, inconsistent, and certain to feel remorse as they are, do nevertheless receive great pleasure, and we must allow that in so doing they are as far from feeling any trouble as they are from forming a right judgment, and that, as is the case with many people, they are possessed by a merry madness, and laugh while they rave. The pleasures of wise men, on the other hand, are mild, decorous, verging on dulness, kept under restraint and scarcely noticeable, and are neither invited to come nor received with honour when they come of their own accord, nor are they welcomed with any delight by those whom they visit, who mix them up with their lives and fill up empty spaces with them, like an amusing farce in the intervals of serious business.
happy-life_section-12.plainEnglish: "They feel uneasy," he says, "because so many things pull their thoughts in different directions. Their minds are disturbed by conflicting ideas." I admit this is true. But these same people — foolish, inconsistent, and bound to regret their choices — still get great pleasure from life. We have to acknowledge that while they're doing this, they feel no trouble at all. They may have terrible judgment, but like many people, they're caught up in a kind of happy madness. They laugh even while they're acting crazy. The pleasures of wise people, on the other hand, are gentle and proper. They border on dullness. They're kept under control and barely noticeable. Wise people don't invite these pleasures in, and when pleasures show up on their own, they don't welcome them with honor or delight. Instead, they mix them into their daily lives and use them to fill empty moments — like light entertainment between serious work.

happy-life_section-12.originalText: Let them no longer, then, join incongruous matters together, or connect pleasure with virtue, a mistake whereby they court the worst of men. The reckless profligate, always in liquor and belching out the fumes of wine, believes that he lives with virtue, because he knows that he lives with pleasure, for he hears it said that pleasure cannot exist apart from virtue; consequently he dubs his vices with the title of wisdom and parades all that he ought to conceal. So, men are not encouraged by Epicurus to run riot, but the vicious hide their excesses in the lap of philosophy, and flock to the schools in which they hear the praises of pleasure.
happy-life_section-12.plainEnglish: So let's stop mixing things that don't belong together. Don't connect pleasure with virtue — that's a mistake that attracts the worst people. The reckless drunk, always drinking and reeking of wine, thinks he's living virtuously because he knows he's living for pleasure. He's heard that pleasure can't exist without virtue. So he calls his vices 'wisdom' and shows off everything he should hide. Epicurus doesn't encourage people to go wild. But bad people use philosophy as a cover for their excesses. They flock to schools where they hear pleasure being praised.

happy-life_section-12.originalText: They do not consider how sober and temperate—for so, by Hercules, I believe it to be—that "pleasure" of Epicurus is, but they rush at his mere name, seeking to obtain some protection and cloak for their vices. They lose, therefore, the one virtue which their evil life possessed, that of being ashamed of doing wrong: for they praise what they used to blush at, and boast of their vices. Thus modesty can never reassert itself, when shameful idleness is dignified with an honourable name. The reason why that praise which your school lavishes upon pleasure is so hurtful, is because the honourable part of its teaching passes unnoticed, but the degrading part is seen by all.
happy-life_section-12.plainEnglish: They don't realize how sober and moderate Epicurus's idea of 'pleasure' really is — and by God, I believe it is moderate. Instead, they just hear his name and rush toward it. They want some excuse and cover for their bad behavior. So they lose the one good thing their wicked lives still had: the shame they felt when doing wrong. Now they praise what used to make them blush. They brag about their vices. Once shame is gone, it can never come back — especially when you give lazy indulgence a respectable name. The problem with your school's praise of pleasure is this: the noble parts of the teaching go unnoticed, but everyone sees the degrading parts.

happy-life_section-13.originalText: I myself believe, though my Stoic comrades would be unwilling to hear me say so, that the teaching of Epicurus was upright and holy, and even, if you examine it narrowly, stern: for this much talked of pleasure is reduced to a very narrow compass, and he bids pleasure submit to the same law which we bid virtue do—I mean, to obey nature. Luxury, however, is not satisfied with what is enough for nature.
happy-life_section-13.plainEnglish: I believe — though my fellow Stoics wouldn't like to hear me say this — that Epicurus taught something good and pure. In fact, if you look closely, his teaching was quite strict. His famous idea about pleasure actually has very tight limits. He said pleasure should follow the same rule we Stoics say virtue should follow — obey nature. But luxury isn't satisfied with what nature actually needs.

happy-life_section-13.originalText: What is the consequence? Whoever thinks that happiness consists in lazy sloth, and alternations of gluttony and profligacy, requires a good patron for a bad action, and when he has become an Epicurean, having been led to do so by the attractive name of that school, he follows, not the pleasure which he there hears spoken of, but that which he brought thither with him, and, haying learned to think that his vices coincide with the maxims of that philosophy, he indulges in them no longer timidly and in dark corners, but boldly in the face of day.
happy-life_section-13.plainEnglish: What happens then? Anyone who thinks happiness means lazy lounging around, stuffing yourself with food, and living wildly needs a good excuse for bad behavior. When he becomes an Epicurean — drawn in by that appealing school name — he doesn't follow the real pleasure they teach about. Instead, he follows the pleasure he already had in mind. Once he convinces himself that his bad habits match their philosophy, he stops being sneaky about his vices. He flaunts them openly in broad daylight.

happy-life_section-13.originalText: I will not, therefore, like most of our school, say that the sect of Epicurus is the teacher of crime, but what I say is: it is ill spoken of, it has a bad reputation, and yet it does not deserve it. "Who can know this without having been admitted to its inner mysteries?" Its very outside gives opportunity for scandal, and encourages men's baser desires: it is like a brave man dressed in a woman's gown: your chastity is assured, your manhood is safe, your body is submitted to nothing disgraceful, but your hand holds a drum (like a priest of Cybele).
happy-life_section-13.plainEnglish: I won't follow most of my fellow Stoics and say that Epicurus teaches people to be criminals. But here's what I will say: his philosophy has a terrible reputation. And honestly? It doesn't deserve that reputation. "But how can you know this unless you've studied it deeply?" The problem is how it looks from the outside. It gives people an excuse to indulge their worst impulses. It's like seeing a brave soldier dressed in women's clothes. You know he's still honorable and strong underneath. Nothing shameful has actually happened to him. But there he is, holding a tambourine like some religious dancer.

happy-life_section-13.originalText: Choose, then, some honourable superscription for your school, some writing which shall in itself arouse the mind: that which at present stands over your door has been invented by the vices. He who ranges himself on the side of virtue gives thereby a proof of a noble disposition: he who follows pleasure appears to be weakly, worn out, degrading his manhood, likely to fall into infamous vices unless someone discriminates his pleasures for him, so that he may know which remain within the bounds of natural desire, which are frantic and boundless, and become all the more insatiable the more they are satisfied.
happy-life_section-13.plainEnglish: Choose a noble motto for your school of philosophy. Pick something that will inspire the mind. The sign over your door right now was created by vice itself. When someone sides with virtue, they show they have a noble character. But someone who chases pleasure looks weak, worn out, and degraded. They're destroying their own humanity and heading toward shameful vices — unless someone helps them sort out their pleasures. They need to learn which desires stay within natural limits and which ones are wild and endless. The crazy ones only get stronger the more you feed them.

happy-life_section-13.originalText: But come! let virtue lead the way: then every step will be safe. Too much pleasure is hurtful: but with virtue we need fear no excess of any kind, because moderation is contained in virtue herself. That which is injured by its own extent cannot be a good thing: besides, what better guide can there be than reason for beings endowed with a reasoning nature? so if this combination pleases you, if you are willing to proceed to a happy life thus accompanied, let virtue lead the way, let pleasure follow and hang about the body like a shadow: it is the part of a mind incapable of great things to hand over virtue, the highest of all qualities, as a handmaid to pleasure.
happy-life_section-13.plainEnglish: But listen! Let virtue lead the way, and every step will be safe. Too much pleasure hurts us. But with virtue, we don't need to fear any kind of excess. Virtue naturally contains moderation within itself. Anything that gets damaged by having too much of it can't be truly good. And what better guide could there be than reason? After all, we're reasoning creatures. So if this combination appeals to you — if you want to reach a happy life this way — then let virtue lead. Let pleasure follow behind like a shadow hanging around the body. Only a mind incapable of great things would make virtue into pleasure's servant. Virtue is the highest quality we have.

happy-life_section-14.originalText: Let virtue lead the way and bear the standard: we shall have pleasure for all that, but we shall be her masters and controllers; she may win some concessions from us, but will not force us to do anything. On the contrary, those who have permitted pleasure to lead the van, have neither one nor the other: for they lose virtue altogether, and yet they do not possess pleasure, but are possessed by it, and are either tortured by its absence or choked by its excess, being wretched if deserted by it, and yet more wretched if overwhelmed by it, like those who are caught in the shoals of the Syrtes and at one time are left on dry ground and at another tossed on the flowing waves.
happy-life_section-14.plainEnglish: Let virtue lead the way and carry the flag. We'll still have pleasures, but we'll be in charge of them. Pleasure might win a few small battles with us, but it won't force us to do anything. But people who let pleasure take the lead? They end up with neither virtue nor pleasure. They lose virtue completely. And they don't really possess pleasure — pleasure possesses them. They're tortured when they can't get it, and choked when they have too much. They're miserable when pleasure leaves them, and even more miserable when it overwhelms them. They're like ships caught in the dangerous shoals of the Syrtes — sometimes stranded on dry sand, sometimes tossed around by crashing waves.

happy-life_section-14.originalText: This arises from an exaggerated want of self-control, and a hidden love of evil: for it is dangerous for one who seeks after evil instead of good to attain his object. As we hunt wild beasts with toil and peril, and even when they are caught find them an anxious possession, for they often tear their keepers to pieces, even so are great pleasures: they turn out to be great evils and take their owners prisoner. The more numerous and the greater they are, the more inferior and the slave of more masters does that man become whom the vulgar call a happy man.
happy-life_section-14.plainEnglish: This happens because people lack self-control and secretly love what's bad for them. It's dangerous when someone who chases evil instead of good actually gets what they want. Think about hunting wild animals — it's hard and risky work, and even after you catch them, they're nothing but trouble. They often attack their own keepers. That's exactly what great pleasures are like. They turn into great evils and make prisoners of their owners. The more pleasures you have, and the bigger they are, the more you become a slave with many masters. Yet ordinary people call this person happy.

happy-life_section-14.originalText:
I may even press this analogy further: as the man who tracks wild animals to their lairs, and who sets great store on—

"Seeking with snares the wandering brutes to noose,"

and

"Making their hounds the spacious glade surround,"

that he may follow their tracks, neglects far more desirable things, and leaves many duties unfulfilled, so he who pursues pleasure postpones everything to it, disregards that first essential, liberty, and sacrifices it to his belly; nor does he buy pleasure for himself, but sells himself to pleasure.
happy-life_section-14.plainEnglish: Let me push this comparison even further. Think of a hunter tracking wild animals to their hiding places. He values highly "catching wandering beasts with snares" and "making his hounds surround the wide clearing" so he can follow their tracks. But while he does this, he ignores far better things and leaves many important duties undone. In the same way, someone who chases pleasure puts everything else second to it. He ignores the most essential thing — his freedom — and sacrifices it to his appetites. He doesn't buy pleasure for himself. He sells himself to pleasure.

happy-life_section-15.originalText: "But what," asks our adversary, "is there to hinder virtue and pleasure being combined together, and a highest good being thus formed, so that honour and pleasure may be the same thing?" Because nothing except what is honourable can form a part of honour, and the highest good would lose its purity if it were to see within itself anything unlike its own better part. Even the joy which arises from virtue, although it be a good thing, yet is not a part of absolute good, any more than cheerfulness or peace of mind, which are indeed good things, but which merely follow the highest good, and do not contribute to its perfection, although they are generated by the noblest causes.
happy-life_section-15.plainEnglish: "But what," our opponent asks, "stops us from combining virtue and pleasure? Why can't we create the highest good by mixing honor and pleasure together?" Here's why: only honorable things can be part of honor. The highest good would lose its purity if it contained anything unlike its best part. Even the joy that comes from virtue — though it's a good thing — isn't part of the absolute good. Neither are cheerfulness or peace of mind. These are good things, but they just follow from the highest good. They don't make it more perfect, even though they come from the noblest causes.

happy-life_section-15.originalText: Whoever on the other hand forms an alliance, and that, too, a one-sided one, between virtue and pleasure, clogs whatever strength the one may possess by the weakness of the other, and sends liberty under the yoke, for liberty can only remain unconquered as long as she knows nothing more valuable than herself: for he begins to need the help of Fortune, which is the most utter slavery: his life becomes anxious, full of suspicion, timorous, fearful of accidents, waiting in agony for critical moments of time. You do not afford virtue a solid immoveable base if you bid it stand on what is unsteady: and what can be so unsteady as dependence on mere chance, and the vicissitudes of the body and of those things which act on the body?
happy-life_section-15.plainEnglish: But anyone who tries to combine virtue with pleasure — and it's always a one-sided alliance — weakens virtue by mixing it with something weak. This puts freedom under the yoke. Freedom can only stay unconquered when it values nothing more than itself. Once you need pleasure, you start needing Fortune's help. And that's complete slavery. Your life becomes anxious, suspicious, timid, afraid of setbacks. You live in agony waiting for crucial moments. You can't give virtue a solid foundation if you tell it to stand on something shaky. And what could be shakier than depending on chance and the ups and downs of the body and everything that affects the body?

happy-life_section-15.originalText: How can such a man obey God and receive everything which comes to pass in a cheerful spirit, never complaining of fate, and putting a good construction upon everything that befalls him, if he be agitated by the petty pin-pricks of pleasures and pains? A man cannot be a good protector of his country, a good avenger of her wrongs, or a good defender of his friends, if he be inclined to pleasures.
happy-life_section-15.plainEnglish: How can a man serve God and accept whatever happens with a cheerful heart? How can he never complain about his fate and see the good in everything that befalls him if he gets upset by tiny pleasures and pains? A man can't protect his country well, or fight for justice, or defend his friends if he's always chasing after pleasures.

happy-life_section-15.originalText: Let the highest good, then, rise to that height from whence no force can dislodge it, whither neither pain can ascend, nor hope, nor fear, nor anything else that can impair the authority of the "highest good." Thither virtue alone can make her way: by her aid that hill must be climbed: she will bravely stand her ground and endure whatever may befal her not only resignedly, but even willingly: she will know that all hard times come in obedience to natural laws, and like a good soldier she will bear wounds, count scars, and when transfixed and dying will yet adore the general for whom she falls: she will bear in mind the old maxim "Follow God."
happy-life_section-15.plainEnglish: Let the highest good rise to a place where nothing can knock it down. A place where pain cannot reach, where hope and fear cannot touch it, where nothing can weaken what makes it the "highest good." Only virtue can reach that high ground. She must help us climb that hill. Once there, virtue will stand firm and face whatever comes — not just with resignation, but willingly. She knows that hard times follow natural laws. Like a good soldier, she will bear her wounds and count her scars. Even when pierced through and dying, she will still love the general she dies for. She will remember the old saying: "Follow God."

happy-life_section-15.originalText: On the other hand, he who grumbles and complains and bemoans himself is nevertheless forcibly obliged to obey orders, and is dragged away, however much against his will, to carry them out: yet what madness is it to be dragged rather than to follow? as great, by Hercules, as it is folly and ignorance of one's true position to grieve because one has not got something or because something has caused us rough treatment, or to be surprised or indignant at those ills which befall good men as well as bad ones, I mean diseases, deaths, illnesses, and the other cross accidents of human life.
happy-life_section-15.plainEnglish: On the other hand, someone who grumbles and complains and feels sorry for himself is still forced to obey fate's orders. He gets dragged along to do what must be done, no matter how much he fights it. But what madness is it to be dragged rather than to go willingly? It's just as crazy, I swear, as it is foolish and ignorant to grieve because you didn't get something you wanted, or because something treated you harshly. It's equally foolish to be surprised or angry at the troubles that hit good people and bad people alike — I mean sickness, death, illness, and all the other painful accidents of human life.

happy-life_section-15.originalText: Let us bear with magnanimity whatever the system of the universe makes it needful for us to bear: we are all bound by this oath: "To bear the ills of mortal life, and to submit with a good grace to what we cannot avoid." We have been born into a monarchy: our liberty is to obey God.
happy-life_section-15.plainEnglish: Let us accept with courage whatever the universe requires us to endure. We are all bound by the same promise: to bear the troubles of human life and submit gracefully to what we cannot change. We were born into a kingdom where God rules. Our freedom comes from obeying God.

happy-life_section-16.originalText: True happiness, therefore, consists in virtue: and what will this virtue bid you do? Not to think anything bad or good which is connected neither with virtue nor with wickedness: and in the next place, both to endure unmoved the assaults of evil, and, as far as is right, to form a god out of what is good. What reward does she promise you for this campaign? an enormous one, and one that raises you to the level of the gods: you shall be subject to no restraint and to no want; you shall be free, safe, unhurt; you shall fail in nothing that you attempt; you shall be debarred from nothing; everything shall turn out according to your wish; no misfortune shall befal you; nothing shall happen to you except what you expect and hope for.
happy-life_section-16.plainEnglish: True happiness comes from virtue. What does virtue tell you to do? First, don't label things as good or bad unless they actually involve virtue or vice. Second, stay calm when bad things happen to you. And when good things come your way, use them properly — almost like making yourself into a god. What does virtue promise in return for this effort? Something huge — it lifts you to the level of the gods. You won't be held back by anything or lack anything you need. You'll be free, safe, and untouchable. You won't fail at what you try. Nothing will be off limits to you. Everything will go your way. No disasters will hit you. Nothing will happen except what you expect and hope for.

happy-life_section-16.originalText: "What! does virtue alone suffice to make you happy?" why, of course, consummate and god-like virtue such as this not only suffices, but more than suffices: for when a man is placed beyond the reach of any desire, what can he possibly lack? if all that he needs is concentred in himself, how can he require anything from without?
happy-life_section-16.plainEnglish: "What! Does virtue alone make you happy?" Of course it does. Perfect, godlike virtue doesn't just make you happy — it gives you more than enough. When you're beyond the reach of any craving, what could you possibly be missing? If everything you need is already inside you, why would you need anything from the outside world?

happy-life_section-16.originalText: He, however, who is only on the road to virtue, although he may have made great progress along it, nevertheless needs some favour from fortune while he is still struggling among mere human interests, while he is untying that knot, and all the bonds which bind him to mortality. What, then, is the difference between them? it is that some are tied more or less tightly by these bonds, and some have even tied themselves with them as well; whereas he who has made progress towards the upper regions and raised himself upwards drags a looser chain, and though not yet free, is yet as good as free.
happy-life_section-16.plainEnglish: Someone who is still learning to be virtuous — even if they've made great progress — still needs some luck from fortune. They're still wrestling with everyday human problems. They're still untying the knot and breaking all the chains that bind them to mortal life. So what's the difference between people? Some are tied more tightly by these chains, and some have even tied themselves up with extra chains. But the person who has made progress toward higher things and lifted themselves up? They drag a looser chain. They're not free yet, but they're as good as free.

happy-life_section-17.originalText: If, therefore, any one of those dogs who yelp at philosophy were to say, as they are wont to do, "Why, then, do you talk so much more bravely than you live? why do you check your words in the presence of your superiors, and consider money to be a necessary implement? why are you disturbed when you sustain losses, and weep on hearing of the death of your wife or your friend? why do you pay regard to common rumour, and feel annoyed by calumnious gossip? why is your estate more elaborately kept than its natural use requires? why do you not dine according to your own maxims? why is your furniture smarter than it need be? why do you drink wine that is older than yourself? why are your grounds laid out?
happy-life_section-17.plainEnglish: So if one of those critics who attack philosophy were to say what they always say: "Why don't you live as boldly as you talk? Why do you watch your words around powerful people? Why do you think money is necessary? Why do you get upset when you lose something, or cry when your wife or friend dies? Why do you care about your reputation and get annoyed by gossip? Why is your estate fancier than it needs to be? Why don't you eat simple meals like you preach? Why is your furniture nicer than necessary? Why do you drink wine older than you are? Why do you have fancy gardens?

happy-life_section-17.originalText: why do you plant trees which afford nothing except shade? why does your wife wear in her ears the price of a rich man's house? why are your children at school dressed in costly clothes? why is it a science to wait upon you at table? why is your silver plate not set down anyhow or at random, but skilfully disposed in regular order, with a superintendent to preside over the carving of the viands?" Add to this, if you like, the questions "Why do you own property beyond the seas? why do you own more than you know of? it is a shame to you not to know your slaves by sight: for you must be very neglectful of them if you only own a few, or very extravagant if you have too many for your memory to retain."
happy-life_section-17.plainEnglish: Why do you plant trees that only give shade? Why does your wife wear earrings worth more than a rich man's house? Why do your children wear expensive clothes to school? Why do you need an expert just to serve you dinner? Why isn't your silverware just placed anywhere, but carefully arranged in perfect order with a special person in charge of carving the meat? Add these questions too: Why do you own property overseas? Why do you own more than you can even keep track of? You should be ashamed that you don't recognize your own slaves. Either you're careless because you only have a few, or you're wasteful because you have too many to remember.

happy-life_section-17.originalText: I will add some reproaches afterwards, and will bring more accusations against myself than you think of: for the present I will make you the following answer. "I am not a wise man, and I will not be one in order to feed your spite: so do not require me to be on a level with the best of men, but merely to be better than the worst: I am satisfied, if every day I take away something from my vices and correct my faults. I have not arrived at perfect soundness of mind, indeed, I never shall arrive at it: I compound palliatives rather than remedies for my gout, and am satisfied if it comes at rarer intervals and does not shoot so painfully. Compared with your feet, which are lame, I am a racer." I make this speech, not on my own behalf, for I am steeped in vices of every kind, but on behalf of one who has made some progress in virtue.
happy-life_section-17.plainEnglish: I'll criticize myself more harshly later — I'll bring up more faults than you can even think of. But for now, here's my answer: "I'm not a wise man, and I won't pretend to be one just to spite you. So don't expect me to match the greatest people who ever lived. Just expect me to be better than the worst. I'm happy if each day I drop some bad habit and fix some flaw. I haven't reached perfect mental health, and I never will. I treat my spiritual problems like gout — I find ways to ease the pain rather than cure it completely. I'm satisfied if the attacks come less often and hurt less. Compared to your crippled feet, I'm a runner." I'm not saying this to defend myself — I'm drowning in every kind of vice. I'm speaking for someone who has made real progress toward virtue.

happy-life_section-18.originalText:
“You talk one way,” objects our adversary, “and live another.”
You most spiteful of creatures, you who always show the bitterest
hatred to the best of men, this reproach was flung at Plato, at
Epicurus, at Zeno: for all these declared how they ought to live,
not how they did live. I speak of virtue, not of myself, and when
I blame vices, I blame my own first of all: when I have the power,
I shall live as I ought to do: spite, however deeply steeped in
