venom, shall not keep me back from what is best: that poison itself
with which you bespatter others, with which you choke yourselves,
shall not hinder me from continuing to praise that life which
I do not, indeed, lead, but which I know I ought to lead, from
loving virtue and from following after her, albeit a long way behind
her and with halting gait.
happy-life_section-18.plainEnglish: "You talk one way," our critic says, "but live another way." You bitter creature, you who always show the harshest hatred toward the best people — this same attack was thrown at Plato, at Epicurus, at Zeno. All of them taught how we ought to live, not how they actually lived. I speak about virtue, not about myself. When I criticize vices, I criticize my own first. When I'm able, I'll live as I should. But your spite, no matter how poisonous, won't stop me from pursuing what's best. That same venom you splash on others — the same poison that's choking you — won't keep me from praising the life I don't lead but know I should lead. I'll keep loving virtue and following her, even if I'm far behind and stumbling.

happy-life_section-18.originalText:
Am I to expect that evil speaking will
respect anything, seeing that it respected neither Rutilius nor
Cato? Will any one care about being thought too rich by men for
whom Diogenes the Cynic was not poor enough? That most energetic
philosopher fought against all the desires of the body, and was
poorer even than the other Cynics, in that besides haying given up
possessing anything he had also given up asking for anything: yet
they reproached him for not being sufficiently in want: as though
forsooth it were poverty, not virtue, of which he professed knowledge.
happy-life_section-18.plainEnglish: Should I expect gossip and slander to respect anyone? Look — it didn't spare Rutilius or Cato. Why would anyone care about being called too rich by people who thought even Diogenes the Cynic wasn't poor enough? That incredible philosopher fought against every bodily desire. He was poorer than other Cynics — he had given up not just owning things, but even asking for them. Yet people still criticized him for not being poor enough. As if he claimed to be an expert on poverty, not virtue!

happy-life_section-19.originalText:
They say that Diodorus, the Epicurean philosopher, who within these last few days put an end to his life with his own hand, did not act according to the precepts of Epicurus, in cutting his throat: some choose to regard this act as the result of madness, others of recklessness; he, meanwhile, happy and filled with the consciousness of his own goodness, has borne testimony to himself by his manner of departing from life, has commended the repose of a life spent at anchor in a safe harbour, and has said what you do not like to hear, because you too ought to do it:

"I've lived, I've run the race which Fortune set me."
happy-life_section-19.plainEnglish: They say that Diodorus, the Epicurean philosopher, killed himself just a few days ago by cutting his throat. People claim this went against Epicurus's teachings. Some call it madness, others call it recklessness. But Diodorus himself was happy and confident in his own goodness. By the way he chose to die, he showed what he believed about himself. He praised the calm of a life lived safely in harbor. And he said something you don't want to hear — because you should do it too: "I have lived. I have run the race that Fortune gave me."

happy-life_section-19.originalText: You argue about the life and death of another, and yelp at the name of men whom some peculiarly noble quality has rendered great, just as tiny curs do at the approach of strangers: for it is to your interest that no one should appear to be good, as if virtue in another were a reproach to all your crimes. You enviously compare the glories of others with your own dirty actions, and do not understand how greatly to your disadvantage it is to venture to do so: for if they who follow after virtue be greedy, lustful, and fond of power, what must you be, who hate the very name of virtue?
happy-life_section-19.plainEnglish: You argue about whether other people are good or bad, and you bark at the names of men who became great through some noble quality. You're like little dogs yapping at strangers. It serves your purpose that no one should appear to be good — because if someone else is virtuous, it makes all your crimes look worse. You jealously compare other people's achievements with your own dirty deeds. You don't realize how badly this comparison makes you look. If people who actually try to be virtuous still struggle with greed, lust, and power — what does that make you, someone who hates the very idea of virtue?

happy-life_section-19.originalText: You say that no one acts up to his professions, or lives according to the standard which he sets up in his discourses: what wonder, seeing that the words which they speak are brave, gigantic, and able to weather all the storms which wreck mankind, whereas they themselves are struggling to tear themselves away from crosses into which each one of you is driving his own nail. Yet men who are crucified hang from one single pole, but these who punish themselves are divided between as many crosses as they have lusts, but yet are given to evil speaking, and are so magnificent in their contempt of the vices of others that I should suppose that they had none of their own, were it not that some criminals when on the gibbet spit upon the spectators.
happy-life_section-19.plainEnglish: You say that no one lives up to their own words or follows the high standards they preach. What's so surprising about that? Their words are bold and grand — strong enough to survive any storm that destroys ordinary people. But they themselves are struggling to escape from crosses that they've nailed themselves to. At least criminals on crosses hang from just one beam. But these self-torturers are stretched across as many crosses as they have desires. And yet they still trash-talk others and act so superior about other people's vices. You'd think they were perfect, except that even criminals hanging on the gallows sometimes spit on the crowd below.

happy-life_section-20.originalText:
"Philosophers do not carry into effect all that they teach."
No; but they effect much good by their teaching, by the noble
thoughts which they conceive in their minds: would, indeed, that
they could act up to their talk: what could be happier than they
would be? but in the meanwhile you have no right to despise good
sayings and hearts full of good thoughts. Men deserve praise for
engaging in profitable studies, even though they stop short of
producing any results. Why need we wonder if those who begin to
climb a steep path do not succeed in ascending it very high? yet,
if you be a man, look with respect on those who attempt great things,
even though they fall. It is the act of a generous spirit to
proportion its efforts not to its own strength but to that of human
nature, to entertain lofty aims, and to conceive plans which are
too vast to be carried into execution even by those who are endowed
with gigantic intellects, who appoint for themselves the following
rules:
happy-life_section-20.plainEnglish:
"Philosophers don't practice everything they preach."

That's true. But they still do a lot of good through their teaching and the noble ideas they develop. I wish they could live up to all their words — imagine how happy they would be! But you have no right to dismiss good advice and hearts full of good intentions. People deserve credit for taking on worthwhile studies, even if they don't see them through to the end.

Why should we be surprised when people who start climbing a steep mountain don't make it to the top? Still, if you're human, show respect for those who attempt great things, even when they fail. It takes a generous spirit to aim not just for what you can handle, but for what humanity itself might achieve. It means having lofty goals and making plans so big that even people with brilliant minds couldn't fully carry them out — people who set these rules for themselves:

happy-life_section-20.originalText:
I will look upon death or upon a comedy with the same
expression of countenance: I will submit to labours, however great
they may be, supporting the strength of my body by that of
my mind: I will despise riches when I have them as much as when I
have them not; if they be elsewhere I will not be more gloomy, if
they sparkle around me I will not be more lively than I should
otherwise be: whether Fortune comes or goes I will take no notice
of her: I will view all lands as though they belong to me, and my
own as though they belonged to all mankind: I will so live as to
remember that I was born for others, and will thank Nature on this
account: for in what fashion could she have done better for me? she
has given me alone to all, and all to me alone.
happy-life_section-20.plainEnglish: I will face death or a comedy with the same calm expression. I will take on any work, no matter how hard, using my mind to strengthen my body. I will despise riches whether I have them or not. If my wealth is gone, I won't be gloomy. If it surrounds me, I won't be more excited than I should be. Whether Fortune comes or goes, I won't even notice her. I will see all lands as if they belong to me, and my own land as if it belongs to everyone. I will live remembering that I was born to serve others, and I will thank Nature for this. How could she have done better for me? She has given me alone to everyone, and everyone to me alone.

happy-life_section-20.originalText:
Whatever I may
possess, I will neither hoard it greedily nor squander it recklessly.
I will think that I have no possessions so real as those which I
have given away to deserving people: I will not reckon benefits by
their magnitude or number, or by anything except the value set upon
them by the receiver: I never will consider a gift to be a large
one if it be bestowed upon a worthy object. I will do nothing because
of public opinion, but everything because of conscience: whenever
I do anything alone by myself I will believe that the eyes of the
Roman people are upon me while I do it. In eating and drinking my
object shall be to quench the desires of Nature, not to fill and
empty my belly. I will be agreeable with my friends, gentle and
mild to my foes: I will grant pardon before I am asked for it, and
will meet the wishes of honourable men half way: I will bear in
mind that the world is my native city, that its governors are the
gods, and that they stand above and around me, criticizing whatever
I do or say.
happy-life_section-20.plainEnglish: Whatever I own, I won't hoard it like a miser or waste it carelessly. I'll believe that my truest possessions are the ones I've given to people who deserve them. I won't measure my generosity by how much I give or how often — only by how much it means to the person receiving it. No gift is too big if it goes to someone worthy. I won't do things to impress others, but because my conscience tells me it's right. Even when I'm alone, I'll act as if all of Rome is watching me. When I eat and drink, I'll satisfy nature's needs — not stuff myself like a glutton. I'll be kind to my friends and gentle even to my enemies. I'll forgive people before they ask for it, and I'll meet good people halfway. I'll remember that the whole world is my hometown, that the gods are its rulers, and that they're always above and around me, watching everything I do and say.

happy-life_section-20.originalText:
Whenever either Nature demands my breath again, or
reason bids me dismiss it, I will quit this life, calling all to
witness that I have loved a good conscience, and good pursuits;
that no one's freedom, my own least of all, has been impaired through
me." He who sets up these as the rules of his life will soar aloft
and strive to make his way to the gods: of a truth, even though he
fails, yet he

"Fails in a high emprise."[4]
happy-life_section-20.plainEnglish: When nature demands my last breath, or when reason tells me it's time to go, I will leave this life. And I will call everyone to witness that I loved having a clear conscience and pursuing good things. I will say that no one's freedom — especially not my own — was hurt because of me. The person who lives by these rules will soar high and try to reach the gods. Even if he fails, he still 'fails in a high emprise.'

happy-life_section-20.originalText:
But you, who hate both virtue and those who practise it, do nothing
at which we need be surprised, for sickly lights cannot bear the
sun, nocturnal creatures avoid the brightness of day, and at its
first dawning become bewildered and all betake themselves to their
dens together: creatures that fear the light hide themselves in
crevices. So croak away, and exercise your miserable tongues in
reproaching good men: open wide your jaws, bite hard: you will break
many teeth before you make any impression.
happy-life_section-20.plainEnglish: But you, who hate virtue and anyone who tries to be good, are acting exactly as we'd expect. Sick eyes can't stand sunlight. Night creatures run from daylight and scramble back to their holes when dawn breaks. Animals that fear light hide in dark cracks. So go ahead and croak your complaints. Exercise those miserable tongues by attacking good people. Open your jaws wide and bite as hard as you can — you'll break plenty of teeth before you leave so much as a scratch.

happy-life_section-21.originalText: "But how is it that this man studies philosophy and nevertheless lives the life of a rich man? Why does he say that wealth ought to be despised and yet possess it? that life should be despised, and yet live? that health should be despised, and yet guard it with the utmost care, and wish it to be as good as possible? Does he consider banishment to be an empty name, and say, "What evil is there in changing one country for another?" and yet, if permitted, does he not grow old in his native land? does he declare that there is no difference between a longer and a shorter time, and yet, if he be not prevented, lengthen out his life and flourish in a green old age?"
happy-life_section-21.plainEnglish: But wait — how can this man study philosophy while living like a rich person? Why does he say wealth should be despised, yet keep his money? Why does he say life should be despised, yet go on living? Why does he say health doesn't matter, yet take careful care of his body and want to be as healthy as possible? Does he claim exile is meaningless and ask, "What's wrong with trading one country for another?" — yet if he's allowed, doesn't he prefer to grow old in his homeland? Does he declare there's no difference between a long life and a short one — yet if nothing stops him, doesn't he try to live as long as possible and enjoy a healthy old age?

happy-life_section-21.originalText: Marcus Cato, when he was praising Curius and Coruncanius and that century in which the possession of a few small silver coins were an offence which was punished by the Censor, himself owned four million sesterces; a less fortune no doubt, than that of Crassus, but larger than of Cato the Censor. If the amounts be compared, he had outstripped his great-grandfather further than he himself was outdone by Crassus, and if still greater riches had fallen to his lot, he would not have spurned them: for the wise man does not think himself unworthy of any chance presents: he does not love riches, but he prefers to have them; he does not receive them into his spirit, but only into his house: nor does he cast away from him what he already possesses, but keeps them, and is willing that his virtue should receive a larger subject-matter for its exercise.
happy-life_section-21.plainEnglish: Marcus Cato used to praise the old heroes Curius and Coruncanius. He'd talk about that ancient time when owning a few silver coins was scandalous enough to get you censured. But Cato himself owned four million sesterces. Sure, that was less than Crassus had, but it was way more than his ancestor Cato the Censor ever had. If you compare the amounts, Cato had outpaced his great-grandfather by more than Crassus had outpaced him. And if even greater wealth had come his way, he wouldn't have turned it down. A wise person doesn't think he's unworthy of good fortune. He doesn't love money, but he'd rather have it than not. He doesn't let wealth into his heart, just into his house. He doesn't throw away what he already has. He keeps it and welcomes the chance for his virtue to work with more material.

happy-life_section-22.originalText: Who can doubt, however, that the wise man, if he is rich, has a wider field for the development of his powers than if he is poor, seeing that in the latter case the only virtue which he can display is that of neither being perverted nor crushed by his poverty, whereas if he has riches, he will have a wide field for the exhibition of temperance, generosity, laboriousness, methodical arrangement, and grandeur.
happy-life_section-22.plainEnglish: Who can doubt that a wise person with money has more ways to develop their character than someone who's poor? When you're poor, the only virtue you can really show is not letting poverty corrupt you or break your spirit. But if you have wealth, you get to practice temperance, generosity, hard work, good planning, and greatness of spirit.

happy-life_section-22.originalText: The wise man will not despise himself, however short of stature he may be, but nevertheless he will wish to be tall: even though he be feeble and one-eyed he may be in good health, yet he would prefer to have bodily strength, and that too, while he knows all the while that he has something which is even more powerful: he will endure illness, and will hope for good health: for some things, though they may be trifles compared with the sum total, and though they may be taken away without destroying the chief good, yet add somewhat to that constant cheerfulness which arises from virtue.
happy-life_section-22.plainEnglish: A wise person won't hate himself for being short, but he'll still wish he were taller. Even if he's weak and has only one eye, he might be content with his health, but he'd rather be strong. He knows he has something more important than physical strength. He'll bear illness patiently, but still hope to get well. Some things don't matter much compared to what's really important. You can lose them without losing the main good in life. But they do add a little something to the steady happiness that comes from virtue.

happy-life_section-22.originalText: Riches encourage and brighten up such a man just as a sailor is delighted at a favourable wind that bears him on his way, or as people feel pleasure at a fine day or at a sunny spot in the cold weather. What wise man, I mean of our school, whose only good is virtue, can deny that even these matters which we call neither good nor bad have in themselves a certain value, and that some of them are preferable to others? to some of them we show a certain amount of respect, and to some a great deal. Do not, then, make any mistake: riches belong to the class of desirable things.
happy-life_section-22.plainEnglish: Wealth makes a person like this happy and energetic. It's like a sailor who feels great when a good wind pushes his ship forward. Or like people who enjoy a beautiful day or find a warm, sunny spot when it's cold outside. What wise person from our school — who believes that virtue is the only true good — would deny this? Even the things we call neither good nor bad have some value. Some are better than others. We respect some of them a little, others a lot. So don't be confused about this: wealth belongs in the category of things worth wanting.

happy-life_section-22.originalText: "Why then," say you, "do you laugh at me, since you place them in the same position that I do?" Do you wish to know how different the position is in which we place them? If my riches leave me, they will carry away with them nothing except themselves: you will be bewildered and will seem to be left without yourself if they should pass away from you: with me riches occupy a certain place, but with you they occupy the highest place of all. In fine, my riches belong to me, you belong to your riches.
happy-life_section-22.plainEnglish: "Why then," you ask, "do you laugh at me if you value riches the same way I do?" Do you want to know how our positions are actually different? If my wealth disappears, it only takes itself with it. But if your wealth disappears, you'll be lost and confused — like you've lost part of yourself. For me, money has a place in my life. For you, it has the most important place. In short, I own my riches. Your riches own you.

happy-life_section-23.originalText: Cease, then, forbidding philosophers to possess money: no one has condemned wisdom to poverty. The philosopher may own ample wealth, but will not own wealth that which has been torn from another, or which is stained with another's blood: his must be obtained without wronging any man, and without its being won by base means; it must be alike honourably come by and honourably spent, and must be such as spite alone could shake its head at. Raise it to whatever figure you please, it will still be an honourable possession, if, while it includes much which every man would like to call his own, there be nothing which any one can say is his own.
happy-life_section-23.plainEnglish: Stop telling philosophers they shouldn't have money. No one ever said that wisdom requires poverty. A philosopher can own plenty of wealth — but not wealth stolen from others or stained with blood. His money must be earned without harming anyone and without using shameful methods. It must be gained honorably and spent honorably. It should be the kind of wealth that only jealous people would criticize. Make it as large as you want — it will still be honorable wealth if it includes many things that everyone would want to own, but nothing that anyone can rightfully claim was taken from them.

happy-life_section-23.originalText: Such a man will not forfeit his right to the favour of Fortune, and will neither boast of his inheritance nor blush for it if it was honourably acquired: yet he will have something to boast of, if he throw his house open, let all his countrymen come among his property, and say, "If any one recognizes here anything belonging to him, let him take it." What a great man, how excellently rich will he be, if after this speech he possesses as much as he had before! I say, then, that if he can safely and confidently submit his accounts to the scrutiny of the people, and no one can find in them any item upon which he can lay hands, such a man may boldly and unconcealedly enjoy his riches.
happy-life_section-23.plainEnglish: This kind of person won't give up his right to good fortune. He won't brag about what he inherited, but he won't be ashamed of it either — as long as he got it honestly. But he will have something to brag about if he opens his house to everyone, lets all his fellow citizens walk through his property, and says, "If anyone sees anything here that belongs to them, take it." What a great man! How truly wealthy he would be if, after saying this, he still owns everything he had before! So I say this: if he can safely and confidently let the people examine his finances, and no one can find anything they can claim as their own, then this man can boldly and openly enjoy his wealth.

happy-life_section-23.originalText: The wise man will not allow a single ill-won penny to cross his threshold: yet he will not refuse or close his door against great riches, if they are the gift of fortune and the product of virtue: what reason has he for grudging them good quarters: let them come and be his guests: he will neither brag of them nor hide them away: the one is the part of a silly, the other of a cowardly and paltry spirit, which, as it were, muffles up a good thing in its lap. Neither will he, as I said before, turn them out of his house: for what will he say? will he say, "You are useless," or "I do not know how to use riches?" As he is capable of performing a journey upon his own feet, but yet would prefer to mount a carriage, just so he will be capable of being poor, yet will wish to be rich; he will own wealth, but will view it as an uncertain possession which will some day fly away from him.
happy-life_section-23.plainEnglish: The wise man won't let a single dirty penny into his house. But he won't slam the door on great wealth if fortune gives it to him honestly and he earned it through virtue. Why should he begrudge money a good home? Let it come in and stay as his guest. He won't brag about it or hide it away. Bragging shows a foolish spirit. Hiding it shows a cowardly, small spirit — like someone clutching a good thing to their chest under a blanket. And he won't kick wealth out of his house either, as I said before. What would he tell it? "You're useless" or "I don't know how to use riches?" He can walk on his own two feet, but he'd rather ride in a carriage if he can. Same with money — he can handle being poor, but he'd rather be rich. He'll own wealth, but he'll see it as something uncertain that will fly away from him someday.

happy-life_section-23.originalText: He will not allow it to be a burden either to himself or to any one else: he will give it—why do you prick up your ears? why do you open your pockets?—he will give it either to good men or to those whom it may make into good men. He will give it after having taken the utmost pains to choose those who are fittest to receive it, as becomes one who bears in mind that he ought to give an account of what he spends as well as of what he receives. He will give for good and commendable reasons, for a gift ill bestowed counts as a shameful loss: he will have an easily opened pocket, but not one with a hole in it, so that much may be taken out of it, yet nothing may fall out of it.
happy-life_section-23.plainEnglish: The wise man won't let wealth become a burden to himself or anyone else. He will give it away — why are you getting excited? Why are you reaching for your wallet? — he will give it to good people or to those who might become good because of it. He will take great care choosing who deserves his gifts. He remembers that he must account for what he spends just as much as what he receives. He will give for good and worthy reasons. A gift given to the wrong person is just a shameful waste. His pocket will open easily when it should, but it won't have holes in it. Plenty can be taken out when needed, but nothing will fall out by accident.

happy-life_section-24.originalText: He who believes giving to be an easy matter, is mistaken: it offers very great difficulties, if we bestow our bounty rationally, and do not scatter it impulsively and at random. I do this man a service, I requite a good turn done me by that one: I help this other, because I pity him: this man, again, I teach to be no fit object for poverty to hold down or degrade.
happy-life_section-24.plainEnglish: Anyone who thinks giving is easy is wrong. It's actually very difficult if you want to give wisely instead of just throwing money around randomly. I help this person because he did me a favor. I help that one because I feel sorry for him. And I teach this other person so he won't let poverty defeat him or drag him down.

happy-life_section-24.originalText: I shall not give some men anything, although they are in want, because, even if I do give to them they will still be in want: I shall proffer my bounty to some, and shall forcibly thrust it upon others: I cannot be neglecting my own interests while I am doing this: at no time do I make more people in my debt than when I am giving things away. "What?" say you, "do you give that you may receive again?" At any rate I do not give that I may throw my bounty away: what I give should be so placed that although I cannot ask for its return, yet it may be given back to me. A benefit should be invested in the same manner as a treasure buried deep in the earth, which you would not dig up unless actually obliged.
happy-life_section-24.plainEnglish: I won't give anything to some people, even though they need it. Why? Because even if I give to them, they'll still be needy. To others, I'll offer my help freely. To still others, I'll force my help on them whether they want it or not. I can't neglect my own interests while doing all this. I'm never more popular than when I'm giving things away. "What?" you say. "Do you give so you can get something back?" Well, I don't give just to waste my generosity. What I give should be placed where I can't demand it back, but it might still come back to me. A favor should work like buried treasure — you wouldn't dig it up unless you absolutely had to.

happy-life_section-24.originalText: Why, what opportunities of conferring benefits the mere house of a rich man affords? for who considers generous behaviour due only to those who wear the toga? Nature bids me do good to mankind—what difference does it make whether they be slaves or freemen, free-born or emancipated, whether their freedom be legally acquired or betowed by arrangement among friends? Wherever there is a human being, there is an opportunity for a benefit: consequently, money may be distributed even within one's own threshold, and a field may be found there for the practice of freehandedness, which is not so called because it is our duty towards free men, but because it takes its rise in a free-born mind. In the case of the wise man, this never falls upon base and unworthy recipients, and never becomes so exhausted as not, whenever it finds a worthy object, to flow as if its store was undiminished.
happy-life_section-24.plainEnglish: Think about all the chances to help people that exist right in a rich person's house. Who says generous behavior is only for citizens? Nature tells me to do good for all mankind. What difference does it make if they're slaves or free people, born free or freed later, whether their freedom is legal or just arranged between friends? Wherever there's a human being, there's a chance to help them. So you can share your wealth even within your own home. You can practice generosity right there. We call it generosity not because it's our duty to free people, but because it comes from a free mind. For a wise person, this generosity never goes to unworthy people. It never runs dry either — whenever it finds someone worthy, it flows as if nothing was ever given away.

happy-life_section-24.originalText: You have, therefore, no grounds for misunderstanding the honourable, brave, and spirited language which you hear from those who are studying wisdom: and first of all observe this, that a student of wisdom is not the same thing as a man who has made himself perfect in wisdom. The former will say to you, "In my talk I express the most admirable sentiments, yet I am still weltering amid countless ills. You must not force me to act up to my rules: at the present time I am forming myself, moulding my character, and striving to rise myself to the height of a great example. If I should ever succeed in carrying out all that I have set myself to accomplish, you may then demand that my words and deeds should correspond,"
happy-life_section-24.plainEnglish: So you have no reason to misunderstand the noble, brave, and passionate words you hear from people who are studying wisdom. But first, notice this important difference: someone who is learning wisdom is not the same as someone who has already mastered it. The student will tell you, "I talk about wonderful ideals, but I'm still struggling with countless problems. Don't expect me to live up to everything I say just yet. Right now I'm working on myself, shaping my character, and trying to reach the level of the great examples I admire. If I ever manage to accomplish everything I've set out to do, then you can demand that my actions match my words."

happy-life_section-24.originalText: But he who has reached the summit of human perfection will deal otherwise with you, and will say, "In the first place, you have no business to allow yourself to sit in judgment upon your betters:" I have already obtained one proof of my righteousness in having become an object of dislike to bad men: however, to make you a rational answer, which I grudge to no man, listen to what I declare, and at what price I value all things. Riches, I say, are not a good thing; for if they were, they would make men good: now since that which is found even among bad men cannot be termed good, I do not allow them to be called so: nevertheless I admit that they are desirable and useful and contribute great comforts to our lives.
happy-life_section-24.plainEnglish: But someone who has reached the peak of human wisdom will handle you differently. He'll say: "First, you have no right to judge your superiors. I already have one proof that I'm on the right path — bad people hate me. But I'll give you a reasonable answer, because I don't refuse to explain myself to anyone. Listen to what I believe and how I value everything. I say riches are not truly good. If they were good, they would make people good. But since even bad people can have wealth, it can't be called truly good. Still, I admit that money is desirable and useful. It does make life much more comfortable."

happy-life_section-25.originalText: Learn, then, since we both agree that they are desirable, what my reason is amongst counting them among good things, and in what respects I should behave differently to you if I possessed them. Place me as master in the house of a very rich man: place me where gold and silver plate is used for the commonest purposes; I shall not think more of myself because of things which even though they are in my house are yet no part of me. Take me away to the wooden bridge and put me down there among the beggars: I shall not despise myself because I am sitting among those who hold out their hands for alms: for what can the lack of a piece of bread matter to one who does not lack the power of dying? Well, then? I prefer the magnificent house to the beggar's bridge.
happy-life_section-25.plainEnglish: Let me explain this, since we both agree these things are desirable. Here's why I count them among good things, and how I'd act differently from you if I had them. Put me in charge of a very rich man's house. Put me where gold and silver dishes are used for everyday meals. I won't think more of myself because of these things. Even though they're in my house, they're not part of who I am. Now take me away to the wooden bridge and drop me there among the beggars. I won't despise myself because I'm sitting among people who hold out their hands for money. What does it matter if I lack a piece of bread when I don't lack the power to die? So what's my point? I prefer the magnificent house to the beggar's bridge.

happy-life_section-25.originalText: Place me among magnificent furniture and all the appliances of luxury: I shall not think myself any happier because my cloak is soft, because my guests rest upon purple. Change the scene: I shall be no more miserable if my weary head rests upon a bundle of hay, if I lie upon a cushion from the circus, with all the stuffing on the point of coming out through its patches of threadbare cloth. Well, then? I prefer, as far as my feelings go, to show myself in public dressed in woollen and in robes of office, rather than with naked or half-covered shoulders: I should like every day's business to turn out just as I wish it to do, and new congratulations to be constantly following upon the former ones: yet I will not pride myself upon this: change all this good fortune for its opposite, let my spirit be distracted by losses, grief, various kinds of attacks: let no hour pass without some dispute: I shall not on this account, though beset by the greatest miseries, call myself the most miserable of beings, nor shall I curse any particular day, for I have taken care to have no unlucky days.
happy-life_section-25.plainEnglish: Put me in a mansion filled with luxury. I won't think I'm any happier just because my clothes are soft or my guests sit on purple cushions. Now change the scene completely. I won't be more miserable if my tired head rests on a pile of hay, or if I sleep on a torn circus cushion with stuffing poking out through holes in the worn fabric. So what's my point? I do prefer to appear in public wearing fine wool and official robes rather than with bare or half-covered shoulders. I'd like my daily business to go exactly as I want it to, with one success following another. But I won't let this make me proud. Now flip all this good fortune upside down. Let my mind be torn apart by losses, grief, and different kinds of attacks. Let no hour pass without some argument. Even surrounded by the greatest miseries, I still won't call myself the most wretched person alive. I won't curse any particular day, because I've made sure I have no unlucky days.

happy-life_section-25.originalText: What, then, is the upshot of all this? it is that I prefer to have to regulate joys than to stifle sorrows. The great Socrates would say the same thing to you. "Make me," he would say, "the conqueror of all nations: let the voluptuous car of Bacchus bear me in triumph to Thebes from the rising of the sun: let the kings of the Persians receive laws from me: yet I shall feel myself to be a man at the very moment when all around salute me as a God. Straightway connect this lofty height with a headlong fall into misfortune: let me be placed upon a foreign chariot that I may grace the triumph of a proud and savage conqueror: I will follow another's car with no more humility than I showed when I stood in my own. What then? In spite of all this, I had rather be a conqueror than a captive."
happy-life_section-25.plainEnglish: So what's the point of all this? I'd rather have to control my joys than struggle to overcome my sorrows. The great Socrates would tell you the same thing. "Make me," he would say, "the conqueror of all nations. Let Bacchus's luxurious chariot carry me in triumph from the sunrise all the way to Thebes. Let the Persian kings receive their laws from me. Even then, I'll still know I'm just a man, right when everyone around me is calling me a god. Now flip this completely — let me fall headfirst into disaster. Put me on a foreign chariot to decorate some cruel conqueror's triumph. I'll follow behind his chariot with no more shame than I showed when I rode in my own. So what? Even with all this, I'd still rather be the conqueror than the captive."

happy-life_section-25.originalText: I despise the whole dominion of Fortune, but still, if I were given my choice, I would choose its better parts. I shall make whatever befals me become a good thing, but I prefer that what befals me should be comfortable and pleasant and unlikely to cause me annoyance: for you need not suppose that any virtue exists without labour, but some virtues need spurs, while others need the curb. As we have to check our body on a downward path, and to urge it to climb a steep one; so also the path of some virtues leads down hill, that of others uphill.
happy-life_section-25.plainEnglish: I despise everything Fortune controls, but honestly, if I had to choose, I'd pick the good parts. I can turn whatever happens to me into something good, but I'd rather have things that are comfortable and pleasant and don't annoy me. Don't think that virtue comes without effort — but some virtues need to be pushed forward, while others need to be held back. Just like we have to hold our body back on a steep downhill path and push it up a steep climb, some virtues take us downhill and others uphill.

happy-life_section-25.originalText: Can we doubt that patience, courage, constancy, and all the other virtues which have to meet strong opposition, and to trample Fortune under their feet, are climbing, struggling, winning their way up a steep ascent? Why! is it not equally evident that generosity, moderation, and gentleness glide easily downhill? With the latter we must hold in our spirit, lest it run away with us: with the former we must urge and spur it on. We ought, therefore, to apply these energetic, combative virtues to poverty, and to riches those other more thrifty ones which trip lightly along, and merely support their own weight.
happy-life_section-25.plainEnglish: Can we doubt that patience, courage, and steadiness — all the virtues that face strong opposition and crush Fortune under their feet — are climbing a steep mountain? They struggle and fight their way up. But isn't it just as clear that generosity, moderation, and gentleness roll easily downhill? With those easy virtues, we must hold back our spirit so it doesn't run away with us. With the hard virtues, we must push and drive ourselves forward. So we should use these tough, fighting virtues when we're poor. And when we're rich, we should use those other careful virtues that move lightly and just carry their own weight.

happy-life_section-25.originalText: This being the distinction between them, I would rather have to deal with those which I could practise in comparative quiet, than those of which one can only make trial through blood and sweat. "Wherefore," says the sage, "I do not talk one way and live another: but you do not rightly understand what I say: the sound of my words alone reaches your ears, you do not try to find out their meaning."
happy-life_section-25.plainEnglish: Since there's a difference between these types of challenges, I'd rather deal with the ones I can practice in relative peace than those you can only test through blood and sweat. "That's why," says the wise man, "I don't say one thing and do another. But you don't really understand what I'm saying. You only hear the sound of my words — you don't try to figure out what they actually mean."

happy-life_section-26.originalText: "What difference, then, is there between me, who am a fool, and you, who are a wise man?" "All the difference in the world: for riches are slaves in the house of a wise man, but masters in that of a fool. You accustom yourself to them and cling to them as if somebody had promised that they should be yours for ever, but a wise man never thinks so much about poverty as when he is surrounded by riches. No general ever trusts so implicitly in the maintenance of peace as not to make himself ready for a war, which, though it may not actually be waged, has nevertheless been declared; you are rendered over-proud by a fine house, as though it could never be burned or fall down, and your heads are turned by riches as though they were beyond the reach of all dangers and were so great that Fortune has not sufficient strength to swallow them up.
happy-life_section-26.plainEnglish: What's the difference between me, a fool, and you, a wise person? All the difference in the world. Riches are slaves in a wise person's house, but masters in a fool's house. You get used to your wealth and cling to it as if someone promised it would be yours forever. But a wise person thinks most about poverty when surrounded by riches. No general trusts peace so much that he stops preparing for war. War might not come, but it's always been declared. You become arrogant because of your fine house, as if it could never burn down or collapse. Wealth goes to your head as if it were safe from all dangers — as if it were so vast that Fortune herself doesn't have the strength to destroy it.

happy-life_section-26.originalText: You sit idly playing with your wealth and do not foresee the perils in store for it, as savages generally do when besieged, for, not understanding the use of siege artillery, they look on idly at the labours of the besiegers and do not understand the object of the machines which they are putting together at a distance: and this is exactly what happens to you: you go to sleep over your property, and never reflect how many misfortunes loom menacingly around you on all sides, and soon will plunder you of costly spoils, but if one takes away riches from the wise man, one leaves him still in possession of all that is his: for he lives happy in the present, and without fear for the future.
happy-life_section-26.plainEnglish: You sit around playing with your money and don't see the dangers coming for it. You're like savages under siege who don't understand siege weapons. They watch the enemy building machines in the distance but have no idea what those machines are for. That's exactly what you do. You fall asleep on your wealth and never think about all the disasters circling around you, ready to rob you of everything valuable. But if you take money away from a wise person, you still leave them with everything that truly belongs to them. They live happily in the present and don't fear the future.

happy-life_section-26.originalText: The great Socrates, or any one else who had the same superiority to and power to withstand the things of this life, would say, 'I have no more fixed principle than that of not altering the course of my life to suit your prejudices: you may pour your accustomed talk upon me from all sides: I shall not think that you are abusing me, but that you are merely wailing like poor little babies.' This is what the man will say who possesses wisdom, whose mind, being free from vices, bids him reproach others, not because he hates them, but in order to improve them:
happy-life_section-26.plainEnglish: The great Socrates, or anyone else with that kind of strength against life's pressures, would say: 'I have one fixed rule — I won't change how I live just to match your opinions. Go ahead and dump your usual complaints on me from every direction. I won't think you're attacking me. I'll think you're just crying like little babies.' This is what a wise person says. Their mind is free from flaws, so they call out others — not because they hate them, but because they want to help them improve.

happy-life_section-26.originalText: and to this he will add, "Your opinion of me affects me with pain, not for my own sake but for yours, because to hate perfection and to assail virtue is in itself a resignation of all hope of doing well. You do me no harm; neither do men harm the gods when they overthrow their altars: but it is clear that your intention is an evil one and that you will wish to do harm even where you are not able. I bear with your prating in the same spirit in which Jupiter, best and greatest, bears with the idle tales of the poets, one of whom represents him with wings, another with horns, another as an adulterer staying out all night, another is dealing harshly with the gods, another as unjust to men, another as the seducer of noble youths whom he carries off by force, and those, too, his own relatives, another as a parricide and the conqueror of another's kingdom, and that his father's. The only result of such tales is that men feel less shame at committing sin if they believe the gods to be guilty of such actions.
happy-life_section-26.plainEnglish: and he will add, "Your hatred hurts me — not because it affects me personally, but because it hurts you. When you hate what is good and attack virtue, you're giving up all hope of becoming better yourself. You're not harming me. People don't harm the gods when they tear down their altars either. But your intention is clearly evil, and you want to cause damage even when you can't. I put up with your nonsense the same way Jupiter puts up with the silly stories poets tell about him. One poet gives him wings, another gives him horns. One makes him an adulterer who stays out all night. Another shows him treating the gods badly, or being unfair to people. Some make him a seducer who kidnaps noble young men by force — even his own relatives. Others make him a killer of his own father who steals someone else's kingdom. The only effect of these stories is that people feel less ashamed of their own sins when they think the gods act just as badly."

happy-life_section-26.originalText: But although this conduct of yours does not hurt me, yet, for your own sakes, I advise you, respect virtue: believe those who having long followed her cry aloud that what they follow is a thing of might, and daily appears mightier. Reverence her as you would the gods, and reverence her followers as you would the priests of the gods: and whenever any mention of sacred writings is made, _favete linguis_, favour us with silence: this word is not derived, as most people imagine, from _favour_, but commands silence, that divine service may be performed without being interrupted by any words of evil omen. It is much more necessary that you should be ordered to do this, in order that whenever utterance is made by that oracle, you may listen to it with attention and in silence.
happy-life_section-26.plainEnglish: Even though your behavior doesn't hurt me, I still advise you for your own good: respect virtue. Listen to those who have followed her for a long time. They call out that what they follow is powerful — and grows more powerful each day. Honor virtue as you would honor the gods. Honor her followers as you would honor priests. And whenever someone mentions sacred writings, _favete linguis_ — give us your silence. This phrase doesn't come from 'favor,' as most people think. It commands silence so that religious service can happen without being interrupted by unlucky words. It's even more important that you do this when wisdom speaks to you. Listen carefully and quietly to that oracle.

happy-life_section-26.originalText: Whenever any one beats a sistrum,[6] pretending to do so by divine command, any proficient in grazing his own skin covers his arms and shoulders with blood from light cuts, any one crawls on his knees howling along the street, or any old man clad in linen comes forth in daylight with a lamp and laurel branch and cries out that one of the gods is angry, you crowd round him and listen to his words, and each increases the other's wonderment by declaring him to be divinely inspired.
happy-life_section-26.plainEnglish: Watch what happens when someone shakes a rattle and claims a god told them to do it. Or when someone cuts their arms and shoulders until they bleed, pretending it's religious. Or when someone crawls down the street on their knees, howling. Or when some old man dressed in white robes comes out in broad daylight carrying a lamp and laurel branch, shouting that the gods are angry. You all crowd around these people. You hang on their every word. You convince each other that they must be speaking for the gods.

happy-life_section-27.originalText: Behold! from that prison of his, which by entering he cleansed from shame and rendered more honourable than any senate house, Socrates addresses you, saying: "What is this madness of yours? what is this disposition, at war alike with gods and men, which leads you to calumniate virtue and to outrage holiness with malicious accusations? Praise good men, if you are able: if not, pass them by in silence: if indeed you take pleasure in this offensive abusiveness, fall foul of one another: for when you rave against Heaven, I do not say that you commit sacrilege, but you waste your time.
happy-life_section-27.plainEnglish: Look! From his prison cell — which he made more honorable than any senate house just by being there — Socrates speaks to you: "What's wrong with you? Why are you at war with both gods and people? Why do you slander virtue and attack what's sacred with your nasty accusations? If you can praise good people, do it. If you can't, then stay quiet. If you really enjoy being cruel with your words, then attack each other instead. When you rage against Heaven, I'm not saying it's blasphemy — I'm saying you're wasting your time."

happy-life_section-27.originalText: I once afforded Aristophanes with the subject of a jest: since then all the crew of comic poets have made me a mark for their envenomed wit: my virtue has been made to shine more brightly by the very blows which have been aimed at it, for it is to its advantage to be brought before the public and exposed to temptation, nor do any people understand its greatness more than those who by their assaults have made trial of its strength. The hardness of flint is known to none so well as to those who strike it. I offer myself to all attacks, like some lonely rock in a shallow sea, which the waves never cease to beat upon from whatever quarter they may come, but which they cannot thereby move from its place nor yet wear away, for however many years they may unceasingly dash against it. Bound upon me, rush upon me, I will overcome you by enduring your onset: whatever strikes against that which is firm and unconquerable merely injures itself by its own violence.
happy-life_section-27.plainEnglish: I once gave Aristophanes something to joke about. Since then, all the comic poets have made me their target for bitter humor. But their attacks have only made my virtue shine brighter. Virtue benefits from being tested in public and exposed to temptation. No one understands how strong virtue is better than those who have tried to attack it. No one knows how hard flint is better than those who strike it. I offer myself to all attacks, like a lonely rock in shallow water. The waves never stop hitting it from every direction, but they can't move it or wear it away, no matter how many years they keep crashing against it. Come at me, rush at me — I will defeat you by enduring your attack. Whatever strikes something firm and unbeatable only hurts itself with its own force.

happy-life_section-27.originalText: Wherefore, seek some soft and yielding object to pierce with your darts. But have you leisure to peer into other men's evil deeds and to sit in judgment upon anybody? to ask how it is that this philosopher has so roomy a house, or that one so good a dinner? Do you look at other people's pimples while you yourselves are covered with countless ulcers? This is as though one who was eaten up by the mange were to point with scorn at the moles and warts on the bodies of the handsomest men.
happy-life_section-27.plainEnglish: So find some soft target for your attacks instead. But do you really have time to spy on other people's bad behavior and judge everyone? Why ask how this philosopher can afford such a big house, or how that one eats such fancy dinners? You're looking at other people's pimples while you're covered with countless sores. It's like someone eaten up by a skin disease pointing and laughing at the moles and warts on beautiful people.

happy-life_section-27.originalText: Reproach Plato with having sought for money, reproach Aristotle with having obtained it, Democritus with having disregarded it, Epicurus with having spent it: cast Phaedrus and Alcibiades in my own teeth, you who reach the height of enjoyment whenever you get an opportunity of imitating our vices! Why do you not rather cast your eyes around yourselves at the ills which tear you to pieces on every side, some attacking you from without, some burning in your own bosoms? However little you know your own place, mankind has not yet come to such a pass that you can have leisure to wag your tongues to the reproach of your betters.
happy-life_section-27.plainEnglish: Go ahead — criticize Plato for seeking money, Aristotle for getting it, Democritus for ignoring it, Epicurus for spending it. Throw Phaedrus and Alcibiades in my face too, you who seem to get the most joy out of copying our worst habits! Why don't you look around at your own problems instead? They're tearing you apart from every direction — some attacking from outside, others burning inside your own heart. No matter how little you understand your place in the world, humanity hasn't sunk so low that you have time to wag your tongues criticizing people who are better than you.

happy-life_section-28.originalText:
This you do not understand, and you bear a countenance which
does not befit your condition, like many men who sit in the circus
or the theatre without having learned that their home is already
in mourning: but I, looking forward from a lofty standpoint, can
see what storms are either threatening you, and will burst in
torrents upon you somewhat later, or are close upon you and on the
point of sweeping away all that you possess. Why, though you are
hardly aware of it, is there not a whirling hurricane at this moment
spinning round and confusing your minds, making them seek and avoid
the very same things, now raising them aloft and now dashing them
below? . . . . . .”
happy-life_section-28.plainEnglish: You don't understand this.
